arXiv:math/0412044v2 [math.AG] 16 Oct 2006

Local Gröbner fan: polyhedral and computational approach

Rouchdi Bahloul and Nobuki Takayama Address: Institut Camille Jordan, UMR CNRS 5208, Université Claude Bernard - Lyon 1, Bât. Jean Braconnier, 43 Boulevard du 11 novembre 1918, 69622 Villeurbanne, France Email address: bahloul@math.univ-lyon1.fr Address: Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Science, Kobe University, 1-1, Rokkodai, Nada-ku, Kobe 657-8501, Japan Email address: takayama@math.kobe-u.ac.jp
Abstract.

The goal of this paper is to show that the local Gröbner fan is a polyhedral fan for ideals in the ring of power series and the homogenized ring of analytic differential operators. We will also discuss about relations between the local Gröbner fan and the (global) Gröbner fan for a given ideal and algorithms of computing local Gröbner fans. In rings of differential operators, finiteness and convexity of local Gröbner fans were firstly proved by Assi, Castro-Jiménez and Granger. But they did not prove that they are polyhedral fans.

Introduction

The Gröbner fan for a (homogeneous) polynomial ideal was introduced by Mora and Robbiano [MR88]. It was also studied by Sturmfels [St95]. Given an ideal and a weight vector on the variables we are interested in the equivalence class (the Gröbner cone) of the weight vector defined by the equality of the initial ideals. In this case it has been proved that the closure of the Gröbner cones form a polyhedral fan. In the ring of algebraic differential operators, Assi, Castro and Granger [ACG00] studied the structure of the Gröbner cones but they did not prove that it gives rise to a polyhedral fan. This last fact has been proved by Saito, Sturmfels and the second author [SST00].

Is there a similar construction for power series ideals or more generally for ideals in the homogenized ring of analytic differential operators h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0})? Assi, Castro-Jiménez and Granger [ACG01] proved that any standard cone (Gröbner cone) is open, polyhedral and convex and they are in finite number. Since the ring of analytic power series 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0}, as a subring of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0}), is graded, their theorem implies that any standard cone (Gröbner cone) of an ideal in 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0} is open, polyhedral, and convex. We note that this fact has already been remarked by Assi [As93]. However, the importance of polyhedral properties of the fan was not evoked and it will be one of our main purpose here.

The way of discussing about the ring of power series and the homogenized ring of analytic differential operators are analogous. However, we will make separate treatments, because the commutative case is interesting itself and more readers will be interested in.

Historically, analogous constructions to Gröbner fan already appeared in works by Lejeune-Jalabert and Teissier [LT73] with the notion of critical tropism. In DD-module theory, we have the notion of slopes with works by Laurent and Mebkhout [Lau87, Meb96, LM99], see also [ACG96]. Critical tropisms or slopes are in fact contained in the trace of a Gröbner fan or a standard fan on a 22-dimensional space.

Now, as an introductive illustration, let us review the case of a principal ideal in the formal power series ring.

Let ff be a formal power series ∑α∈Ecα​xα\sum_{\alpha\in E}c_{\alpha}x^{\alpha} in nn variables. Here, the set EE is the support of the power series in the space of exponents. The convex polyhedron

New⁡(f)=conv⁡{α+ℕn|α∈E}\mathrm{New}(f)=\mathrm{conv}\{\alpha+\mathbb{N}^{n}|\alpha\in E\}

is called the Newton polyhedron of ff. We are interested in the polyhedral structure of it.

Let uu be a vector in ℝ≤0n\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}^{n}, which we will call a weight vector. For a given weight vector uu, let us consider the height of points of the Newton polyhedron with respect to the direction uu. The set of the highest points of New⁡(f)\mathrm{New}(f)

faceu​(New⁡(f))={α∈New⁡(f)⊂ℝn|u⋅α≥u⋅α′​ for all ​α′∈New⁡(f)}\mathrm{face}_{u}(\mathrm{New}(f))=\{\alpha\in\mathrm{New}(f)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}|u\cdot\alpha\geq u\cdot\alpha^{\prime}\mbox{ for all }\alpha^{\prime}\in\mathrm{New}(f)\}

is called the face of New⁡(f)\mathrm{New}(f) with respect to uu. It is known that there exist only a finite number of faces. For a given face F=faceu​(New​(f))F=\mathrm{face}_{u}(\mathrm{New}(f)), the normal cone of FF is defined by

N⁡(F)={u′∈ℝ≤0n|faceu′​(New⁡(f))=faceu​(New⁡(f))}.\mathrm{N}(F)=\{u^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}^{n}|\mathrm{face}_{u^{\prime}}(\mathrm{New}(f))=\mathrm{face}_{u}(\mathrm{New}(f))\}.

It can be defined in terms of the initial term as follows

(1) N(F)={u′∈ℝ≤0n|inu′(f)=inu(f),supp(u′)=supp(u)},\mathrm{N}(F)=\{u^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}^{n}|\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(f)={\rm in}_{u}(f),\ \mathrm{supp}(u^{\prime})=\mathrm{supp}(u)\},

where supp⁡(u)={i|ui≠0}\mathrm{supp}(u)=\{i\,|\,u_{i}\neq 0\}. The normal cone N⁡(F)\mathrm{N}(F) is an open rational convex polyhedral cone. The collection of the closures of the normal cones

ℰ¯​(f)={N⁡(F)¯| F runs over the faces of New⁡(f)}\bar{\mathcal{E}}(f)=\{\overline{\mathrm{N}(F)}|\mbox{ $F$ runs over the faces of $\mathrm{New}(f)$}\}

is called the normal fan of the Newton polyhedron. Figure 1 illustrates the situation for f⁡(x,y)=x3−y2f(x,y)=x^{3}-y^{2}. It is well-known and fundamental that the normal fan is a polyhedral fan. Let us recall the definition.

Definition 0.0.1.

A polyhedral fan is a finite collection of (closed) polyhedral cones satisfying the following axioms:

  • 1.

    Every face of a cone is again a cone.

  • 2.

    The intersection of any two cones is a face of both.

Can we generalize the results above to ideals and left ideals of differential operators? We can define an analogue of the normal cone by using an equivalence of initial ideals as in (1). Then, it is natural to ask if the collection of the closures of the cones is a polyhedral fan or not. The collection has been called the Gröbner fan or the standard fan. The normal fan defined above is the Gröbner fan of the principal ideal generated by ff.

In case of non-principal ideals, we will see that the Gröbner fan is locally a common refinement of the normal fans of a nice set of generators. Sturmfels introduced this geometric picture of Gröbner fan in case of homogeneous ideals of the polynomial ring [St95]. We will apply his idea to local settings with the help of the division theorem of Assi, Castro-Jiménez and Granger [ACG01]. This division takes place in the homogenized ring of analytic (or formal) differential operators. Such an environment is necessary if we want a division adapted to a general weight vector. Indeed, a general division does not exist in the ring D^\hat{D} of formal differential operators as illustrated with the following example by T. Oaku.

Example 0.0.2.

Take n=1n=1. We want to divide f=xf=x by g=x+xk∂g=x+x^{k}\partial with respect to a weight vector w=(u,v)w=(u,v), with u<0u<0 and u+v≥0u+v\geq 0. Take k≥2k\geq 2 sufficiently large such that x≻xk∂x\succ x^{k}\partial. Here ≺\prec is a refinement of the partial order defined by ww. Suppose that a division theorem holds:

x=q⋅(x+xk∂)+r,q,r∈D^x=q\cdot(x+x^{k}\partial)+r,\quad q,r\in\hat{D}

where rr cannot be divided by gg, i.e. the leading monomial of rr is not divisible by xx the leading monomial of gg. But r=x−q⋅(x+∂xk+k​xk−1)=(1−q−q​∂xk−1−k​xk−2)⋅xr=x-q\cdot(x+\partial x^{k}+kx^{k-1})=(1-q-q\partial x^{k-1}-kx^{k-2})\cdot x therefore the leading monomial of rr contains xx. It is a contradiction.

Finally, let us mention about applications of our result. The first author gave a constructive method to compute a local Bernstein-Sato polynomial for a given set of analytic functions or polynomials in [Ba05]. An essential step of the construction is the computation of an analytic standard fan, and we will give algorithms to compute it. The second application is given by N. Touda who constructs local tropical variety based on our result that “the local Gröbner fan is a polyhedral fan” [To05]. This is an analogous construction of tropical variety by D. Speyer and B. Sturmfels [SS04].

1. Definitions and statement of the main results

We fix an integer n≥1n\geq 1. We denote by xx the system of variables (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}). The partial derivation ∂∂xi\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}} shall be denoted by ∂i\partial_{i}. We will use the notation xαx^{\alpha} for x1α1⋯xnαnx_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\alpha_{n}} where α∈ℕn\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{n}. In the same way ∂β\partial^{\beta} denotes ∂1β1⋯∂nβn\partial_{1}^{\beta_{1}}\cdots\partial_{n}^{\beta_{n}}.

The symbol 𝐤\mathbf{k} denotes a field. 𝐤​[x]0\mathbf{k}[x]_{0} denotes the localization of 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x] at the point 0∈𝐤n0\in\mathbf{k}^{n}. When 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C} this is a subring of 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0} germ at 00 of analytic functions. The latter is itself a subring of the formal power series ring O^=𝐤⁡[[x]]{\hat{O}}=\mathbf{k}[[x]]. In this section, the symbol 𝒞\mathcal{C} shall denote one of the rings 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x], 𝐤​[x]0\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}, 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0}, O^{\hat{O}}.

Now let us denote respectively by DD, D{0}D_{\{0\}}, 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} and D^\hat{D} the ring of differential operators with coefficients in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x], 𝐤​[x]0\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}, 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0} and O^{\hat{O}}. The symbol ℛ\mathcal{R} shall denote one of these rings.

Recall that these rings are characterized by the following relations: for any c⁡(x)∈𝒞c(x)\in\mathcal{C} and i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, ∂ic(x)−c(x)∂i=∂c⁡(x)∂xi\partial_{i}c(x)-c(x)\partial_{i}=\frac{\partial c(x)}{\partial x_{i}}.

We denote by 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} the set {u∈ℝn|ui≤0,∀i}\{u\in\mathbb{R}^{n}|u_{i}\leq 0,\forall i\}. This is a subset of 𝒰glob=ℝn\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}}=\mathbb{R}^{n}. We denote by 𝒲loc={w=(u,v)∈ℝ2​n|ui≤0,ui+vi≥0,∀i}\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}=\{w=(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}|u_{i}\leq 0,u_{i}+v_{i}\geq 0,\forall i\}. This is subset of 𝒲glob={w=(u,v)∈ℝ2​n|ui+vi≥0,∀i}\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{glob}}=\{w=(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}|u_{i}+v_{i}\geq 0,\forall i\}. For each ii, uiu_{i} shall be seen as a weight on the variable xix_{i} while viv_{i} shall be a weight on ∂i\partial_{i}. The use of the subscripts “loc” and “glob” together with the relations ui≤0u_{i}\leq 0 and ui+vi≥0u_{i}+v_{i}\geq 0 shall be made clearer in Remark 1.0.1 (see below).

For the construction of Gröbner fans, we will need a division process with respect to “arbitrary” weight vectors in rings of differential operators. We have seen in Example 0.0.2 that a general division does not exist e.g. in D^\hat{D}. Therefore, homogenization techniques will be necessary. They are differential generalizations of that by Lazard [Laz83].

First let us define the (𝟎,𝟏){(\mathbf{0,1})}-homogenization. Let us introduce the ring h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}). It is the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-algebra generated by O^{\hat{O}}, ∂i\partial_{i} (i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n) and a new variable hh with

∂ic(x)−c(x)∂i=∂c⁡(x)∂xi⋅h,\partial_{i}c(x)-c(x)\partial_{i}=\frac{\partial c(x)}{\partial x_{i}}\cdot h,

i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, as the only non trivial commutation relations. We can replace O^{\hat{O}} by 𝐤⁡[x],𝐤​[x]0,𝒪0\mathbf{k}[x],\mathbf{k}[x]_{0},\mathcal{O}_{0} and we obtain the subrings h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)⊂h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0})⊂h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0)⊂h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D)\subset h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}})\subset h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0})\subset h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}). An element PP in one of these rings has a unique writing as P=∑α,β,kcα,β,k​xα​∂βhkP=\sum_{\alpha,\beta,k}c_{\alpha,\beta,k}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{k}. We define the support Supp⁡(P)⊂ℕ2​n+1\mathrm{Supp}(P)\subset\mathbb{N}^{2n+1} of PP as the set of (α,β,k)(\alpha,\beta,k) such that cα,β,k≠0c_{\alpha,\beta,k}\neq 0. We define its degree deg⁡(P)\deg(P) as the maximum of |β|+k|\beta|+k. We say that PP is homogeneous if for any (α,β,k)(\alpha,\beta,k) in Supp⁡(P)\mathrm{Supp}(P), |β|+k=deg⁡(P)|\beta|+k=\deg(P). An ideal in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(ℛ)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{R}) is said to be homogeneous if it can be generated by homogeneous elements.

Let P=∑α,βcα,βxα∂βP=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta} in ℛ\mathcal{R}. The support Supp⁡(P)⊂ℕ2​n\mathrm{Supp}(P)\subset\mathbb{N}^{2n} is defined in the same way. We define the (𝟎,𝟏){(\mathbf{0,1})}-degree of PP as the maximum of |β||\beta| for (α,β)∈Supp⁡(P)(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathrm{Supp}(P). Its (𝟎,𝟏){(\mathbf{0,1})}-homogenization is defined by h(𝟎,𝟏)​(P)=∑cα,β​xα​∂βhdeg⁡(P)−|β|h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(P)=\sum c_{\alpha,\beta}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{\deg(P)-|\beta|}. It is a homogeneous element of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(ℛ)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{R}) of degree the degree of PP.

Now let us introduce the (𝟏,𝟏){(\mathbf{1,1})}-homogenized Weyl algebra h(𝟏,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(D) ([Ta91], [CN97]). It is the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-algebra generated by the symbols xix_{i}, ∂i\partial_{i} and hh where the only non trivial relations are

∂ixi−xi∂i=h2;i=1,…,n.\partial_{i}x_{i}-x_{i}\partial_{i}=h^{2};\ i=1,\ldots,n.

For P∈h(𝟏,𝟏)​(D)P\in h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(D), its degree shall be the total degree in all the variables. It is homogeneous if all its monomials have the same degree. For P=∑α,βcα,βxα∂βP=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta} in DD, the (𝟏,𝟏){(\mathbf{1,1})}-degree is the total degree in the variables xix_{i} and ∂i\partial_{i}. We define the (𝟏,𝟏){(\mathbf{1,1})}-homogenization of PP as h(𝟏,𝟏)​(P)=∑cα,β​xα​∂βhd−|α|−βh_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(P)=\sum c_{\alpha,\beta}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{d-|\alpha|-\beta} where dd is the (𝟏,𝟏){(\mathbf{1,1})}-degree of PP. This is a homogeneous element of degree dd.

For f∈𝒞f\in\mathcal{C} and a local weight vector u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}, we denote by ordu​(f)\mathrm{ord}^{u}(f) the maximum of the scalar products u⋅αu\cdot\alpha for α∈Supp⁡(f)\alpha\in\mathrm{Supp}(f). In the case f∈𝐤⁡[x]f\in\mathbf{k}[x], this definition is valid for u∈𝒰globu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}}. The order gives rise to a filtration Fu​(𝒞)F^{u}(\mathcal{C}) given by Fku={f|ordu​(f)≤k}F^{u}_{k}=\{f|\mathrm{ord}^{u}(f)\leq k\} as well as to the associated graded ring gru(𝒞)=⊕kFku/F<ku\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C})=\oplus_{k}F_{k}^{u}/F^{u}_{<k}. If 𝒞=𝐤⁡[x]\mathcal{C}=\mathbf{k}[x] and u∈𝒰globu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}}, this graded ring is equal to 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x]. All these rings can be seen as subrings of gru​(O^)\mathrm{gr}^{u}({\hat{O}}). For f∈𝒞f\in\mathcal{C}, its initial form inu​(f)\mathrm{in}_{u}(f) shall be the class of ff in Fku/F<kuF_{k}^{u}/F^{u}_{<k} where k=ordu​(f)k=\mathrm{ord}^{u}(f). In literature, we also find the terminology principal symbol with the notation σu​(f)\sigma^{u}(f). Now if II is an ideal in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the restriction of Fu​(𝒞)F^{u}(\mathcal{C}) to II gives rise to a graded ideal in gru​(𝒞)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}) which we denote by inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I). This ideal is in fact generated by all the inu​(f)\mathrm{in}_{u}(f) for f∈If\in I.

Now all the definitions above are valid if we replace 𝒞\mathcal{C} by ℛ\mathcal{R} and 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} (resp. 𝒰glob\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}}) by 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}} (resp. 𝒲glob\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{glob}}). For example if write w=(u,v)w=(u,v) then ordw​(P)\mathrm{ord}^{w}(P) shall be the maximum of (u,v)⋅(α,β)(u,v)\cdot(\alpha,\beta) for (α,β)∈Supp⁡(P)(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathrm{Supp}(P). Moreover if we put the weight 00 to the variable hh, we can extend the definitions above to h(𝟏,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(D) or h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D) with 𝒲glob\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{glob}} and to h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0})h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}), h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0}), h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}) with 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

Remark 1.0.1.

The subscript “loc” means that we are working with local rings. In this case, the weights uiu_{i} of the xix_{i} variables need to be ≤0\leq 0 if we want the definition above to work. Moreover the conditions ui+vi≥0u_{i}+v_{i}\geq 0 are necessary to respect the non commutative structure of the rings in the differential case. Indeed we have: ordw(xi∂i)=ui+vi\mathrm{ord}^{w}(x_{i}\partial_{i})=u_{i}+v_{i} and ordw(xi)+ordw(∂i)=ui+vi\mathrm{ord}^{w}(x_{i})+\mathrm{ord}^{w}(\partial_{i})=u_{i}+v_{i}. Similarly, we would like to have ordw​(∂ixi)=vi+ui\mathrm{ord}^{w}(\partial_{i}x_{i})=v_{i}+u_{i}. Since ∂ixi=xi∂i+1\partial_{i}x_{i}=x_{i}\partial_{i}+1 and ordw(xi∂i)=ui+vi\mathrm{ord}^{w}(x_{i}\partial_{i})=u_{i}+v_{i} and ordw​(1)=0\mathrm{ord}^{w}(1)=0, we need ui+vi≥0u_{i}+v_{i}\geq 0.

Let uu be in 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} and define a strata in the weight space:

S𝒞​(u)={u∈𝒰loc|gru​(𝒞)=gru′​(𝒞)}.S_{\mathcal{C}}(u)=\{u\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}|\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C})=\mathrm{gr}^{u^{\prime}}(\mathcal{C})\}.

We simply write S⁡(u)S(u) when no confusion arises. Then for a given ideal II in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, consider the equivalence relation

u∼u′⇔u′∈S⁡(u)​ and ​inu​(I)=inu′​(I)u\sim u^{\prime}\iff u^{\prime}\in S(u)\textrm{ and }\mathrm{in}_{u}(I)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(I)

for which we denote by CI​[u]C_{I}[u] the class of uu. This class is called a Gröbner cone (the Gröbner cone of II w.r.t. uu). We then denote by ℰ⁡(I,𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) the set the Gröbner cones CI​[u]C_{I}[u] for u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}. This is the open Gröbner fan of II on 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}. If ℛ=𝐤⁡[x]\mathcal{R}=\mathbf{k}[x], we can do the same by replacing 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} with 𝒰glob\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}} and obtain ℰ⁡(I,𝒰glob)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}}). When the context is clear we shall only write ℰ⁡(I)\mathcal{E}(I) (for example if 𝒞=O^\mathcal{C}={\hat{O}}). The notation ℰ\mathcal{E} comes from the word “éventail”.

Finally, the closure of CI​[u]C_{I}[u] will be called the closed Gröbner cone of II w.r.t. uu. The set of the closed Gröbner cones shall be denoted by ℰ¯​(I,𝒰loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) (resp. ℰ¯​(I,𝒰glob)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}})) and called the closed Gröbner fan of II.

We can give the same definitions for an ideal II in ℛ\mathcal{R}, h(𝟏,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(D) or h(𝟎,𝟏)​(ℛ)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{R}).

Note.

  • •

    In [MR88] Mora and Robbiano introduced and studied the Gröbner fan for a homogeneous ideal in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x]. It has been proved by Sturmfels [St95] that the closed Gröbner fan is a polyhedral fan.

  • •

    In [ACG00], Assi, Castro-Jiménez and Granger introduced ℰ⁡(h(𝟏,𝟏)​(I),𝒲glob)\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{glob}}) for an ideal II in DD and called it the Gröbner fan of II. It is not strictly speaking a fan, although for this case, Saito, Sturmfels and Takayama [SST00] proved that ℰ¯​(J)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(J) is a polyhedral fan for any homogeneous JJ in h(𝟏,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(D).

  • •

    In [ACG01], Assi, Castro-Jiménez and Granger defined and worked with ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) for II in 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} (or D^\hat{D}). They proved it is a finite collection of convex rational polyhedral cones and called it the (analytic) standard fan of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I), however they did not prove that ℰ¯​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I))\bar{\mathcal{E}}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I)) is a polyhedral fan.

Let us state the main contributions of the present paper.

  • (A)

    Let II be an ideal in 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0} or O^{\hat{O}} then the closed Gröbner fan ℰ¯​(I,𝒰loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is a polyhedral fan.

  • (B)

    Let II be a homogeneous ideal in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0}) or h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}) then the closed Gröbner fan ℰ¯​(I,𝒲loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is a polyhedral fan.

  • (C)

    Let II be an ideal in k⁡[x]k[x] then ℰ¯​(𝐤​[x]0​I,𝒰loc)=ℰ¯​(O^​I,𝒰loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}})=\bar{\mathcal{E}}({\hat{O}}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) and we provide an algorithm to compute its restriction to any linear subspace.

  • (D)

    Let II be an ideal in DD then we provide an algorithm to compute the open Gröbner fan of D^​I\hat{D}I and the closed Gröbner fan of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I) (the latter being a fan).

  • (E)

    Comparison theorems of local and global Gröbner fans (Theorems 4.1.6, 4.1.8, 4.2.3, 4.2.4, 5.1.1).

The fan in (C) (resp. (D)) shall be called the local Gröbner fan (at x=0x=0) of II.

The way of discussing about the ring of power series and the homogenized ring of analytic differential operators are analogous. However, we will make separate treatments; in section 2, we discuss about the ring of power series and, in section 3, we only prove the results which are specific to the case of differential operators and we refer to section 2 otherwise. In section 4 we give general results about the different kinds of Gröbner fans and we compare them (E). In section 5 we will be concerned with (C) and (D). Results (A) and (B) will be fundamental for enumerating the Gröbner cones. We end section 5 with some examples.

2. The closed Gröbner fan in O^{\hat{O}} or 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0} is a polyhedral fan

In this section we will prove the following theorem.

Theorem 2.0.1.

Let II be an ideal in 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0} or in O^{\hat{O}} then the closed Gröbner fan ℰ¯​(I,𝒰loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is a rational polyhedral fan.

2.1. Division theorem and standard bases in gru​(O^)\mathrm{gr}^{u}({\hat{O}}) and gru​(𝒪0)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{O}_{0})

In the following, we will state a division theorem in the graded rings gru​(O^)\mathrm{gr}^{u}({\hat{O}}) and gru​(𝒪0)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{O}_{0}), let us describe them more explicitly.

Lemma 2.1.1.

Let u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} be a local weight vector and for some 0≤m≤n0\leq m\leq n assume that u=(u1,…,um,0,…,0)u=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{m},0,\ldots,0) with ui≠0u_{i}\neq 0. Then
gru​(𝒪0)=ℂ⁡{xm+1,…,xn}​[x1,…,xm]\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{O}_{0})=\mathbb{C}\{x_{m+1},\ldots,x_{n}\}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}] and gru​(O^)=𝐤⁡[[xm+1,…,xn]]​[x1,…,xm]\mathrm{gr}^{u}({\hat{O}})=\mathbf{k}[[x_{m+1},\ldots,x_{n}]][x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}].

The proof immediately follows from the definition. Let us denote by 𝒞\mathcal{C} one of O^{\hat{O}}, 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0}. Thanks to the preceding lemma, we shall see gru​(𝒞)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}) as a subring of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. An element f∈𝒞f\in\mathcal{C} is said to be uu-homogeneous (or simply homogeneous if the context is clear) if all its monomials have the same uu-order.

Let ≺\prec be a total order on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n} (or equivalently on the terms xα=x1α1⋯xnαnx^{\alpha}=x_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\alpha_{n}}). It is said to be a monomial order if α≺α′\alpha\prec\alpha^{\prime} implies δ+α≺δ+α′\delta+\alpha\prec\delta+\alpha^{\prime}. It is called local if moreover α⪯0\alpha\preceq 0 for any α\alpha. On the opposite side, a monomial order with α⪰0\alpha\succeq 0 is called a global or a well order.

Let f∈𝒞f\in\mathcal{C} be a non zero power series then we define its leading exponent exp≺⁡(f)\exp_{\prec}(f) w.r.t. ≺\prec as the maximum of Supp⁡(P)\mathrm{Supp}(P) for ≺\prec. We define its leading term lt≺​(f)=xexp≺⁡(f)\mathrm{lt}_{\prec}(f)=x^{\exp_{\prec}(f)}, its leading coefficient lc≺​(f)\mathrm{lc}_{\prec}(f) (in 𝐤\mathbf{k} or ℂ\mathbb{C}) as the coefficient corresponding to lt≺​(f)\mathrm{lt}_{\prec}(f) and its leading monomial lm≺​(f)=lc≺​(f)​lt≺​(f)\mathrm{lm}_{\prec}(f)=\mathrm{lc}_{\prec}(f)\mathrm{lt}_{\prec}(f).

Let us state a division theorem in gru​(𝒞)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}) for ≺\prec with unique quotients and remainder similarly to [CG04].

Let g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} be non zero homogeneous elements in gru​(𝒞)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}). Define a partition of ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n} associated with the exp≺⁡(gj)\exp_{\prec}(g_{j}) as Δ1=exp≺⁡(g1)+ℕn\Delta_{1}=\exp_{\prec}(g_{1})+\mathbb{N}^{n}, Δj=(exp≺⁡(gj)+ℕn)∖(Δ1∪⋯∪Δj−1)\Delta_{j}=(\exp_{\prec}(g_{j})+\mathbb{N}^{n})\smallsetminus(\Delta_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\Delta_{j-1}) for j>1j>1 and Δ¯=ℕn∖(∪jΔj)\bar{\Delta}=\mathbb{N}^{n}\smallsetminus(\cup_{j}\Delta_{j}).

Theorem 2.1.2 (Division theorem in gru​(𝒪0)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{O}_{0}) and gru​(O^)\mathrm{gr}^{u}({\hat{O}})).

For any homogeneous f∈gru​(𝒞)f\in\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}), there exists a unique (q1,…,qr,R)∈gru​(𝒞)r+1(q_{1},\ldots,q_{r},R)\in\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C})^{r+1} made of homogeneous elements such that f=∑jqj​gj+Rf=\sum_{j}q_{j}g_{j}+R and

  • •

    for any jj, either qj=0q_{j}=0 or Supp⁡(qj)+exp≺⁡(gj)⊂Δj\mathrm{Supp}(q_{j})+\exp_{\prec}(g_{j})\subset\Delta_{j},

  • •

    either R=0R=0 or Supp⁡(R)⊂Δ¯\mathrm{Supp}(R)\subset\bar{\Delta}.

We call RR the remainder of the division of ff by the gjg_{j} w.r.t. ≺\prec.

Proof.

Let us first suppose u=(0)u=(0). In this case gru​(𝒞)=𝒞\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C} and any element in 𝒞\mathcal{C} is uu-homogeneous (of order 00). Let us show how we can derive the result from [CG04, Theorem 1.5.1]. By Robbiano’s theorem [Ro85], the order ≺\prec can be defined as a lexicographical order with respect to nn weight vectors. Let w1w^{1} be the first of them. Then define the order <w1<_{w^{1}} in a lexicographical way by w1w^{1} and by <0<_{0} where <0<_{0} is the inverse of ≺\prec (and thus <0<_{0} is a well order). The orders ≺\prec and <w1<_{w^{1}} are equivalent. Since ≺\prec is local w1w^{1} has non positive components. Thus with the order <w1<_{w^{1}}, we are exactly under the hypotheses of [CG04, Theorem 1.5.1]. Now suppose uu is not necessarily zero. Since gru​(𝒞)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}) is a subring of 𝒞\mathcal{C} (by lemma 2.1.1), we make the division in 𝒞\mathcal{C} and we remark that the division process conserves uu-homogeneity which concludes the proof. ∎

As a consequence we have:

exp≺⁡(f)=max≺⁡{exp≺⁡(qj​gj),j=1,…,r;exp≺⁡(R)}\exp_{\prec}(f)=\max_{\prec}\{\exp_{\prec}(q_{j}g_{j}),j=1,\ldots,r;\exp_{\prec}(R)\}.
With the notations of the proof above, this implies the following:

ordw1​(f)=max⁡{ordw1​(qj​gj),j=1,…,r;ordw1​(R)}\mathrm{ord}^{w^{1}}(f)=\max\{\mathrm{ord}^{w^{1}}(q_{j}g_{j}),j=1,\ldots,r;\mathrm{ord}^{w^{1}}(R)\}.

Let JJ be an ideal in gru​(𝒞)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}). We suppose JJ to be uu-homogeneous, i.e. generated by homogeneous elements. We define the set of the leading exponents of JJ as

Exp≺(J)={exp≺(f)|f∈J,f≠0}.\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec}(J)=\{\exp_{\prec}(f)|f\in J,\ f\neq 0\}.

This set is stable by sums in ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n} thus by Dickson lemma:

Definition 2.1.3.

There exists G={g1,…,gr}⊂JG=\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\}\subset J (made of homogeneous elements) such that Exp≺(J)=∪j(exp≺(gj)+ℕn)\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec}(J)=\cup_{j}(\exp_{\prec}(g_{j})+\mathbb{N}^{n}). Such a set GG is called a (homogeneous) ≺\prec-standard basis of JJ.

The statement concerning homogeneity follows from the following: take gj∈Gg_{j}\in G, then any uu-homogeneous part of gg belongs to JJ. Let gj′g^{\prime}_{j} be the one that contains the leading term of gg. The set of gj′g^{\prime}_{j} is a homogeneous standard basis.

The following statements are equivalent, see [CG04, Cor. 1.5.4]:

  • •

    A set G⊂JG\subset J is a homogeneous standard basis of JJ

  • •

    For any homogeneous f∈gru​(𝒞)f\in\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}): f∈Jf\in J if and only if the remainder of the division of ff by GG is zero.

Keeping the notations of the proof above, we see that for such a standard basis, the set of inw1​(g)\mathrm{in}_{w^{1}}(g) for g∈Gg\in G generates inw1​(J)\mathrm{in}_{w^{1}}(J). In fact we have more than that: Given a local order ≺\prec and u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}, we define the local order ≺u\prec_{u} in a lexicographical way by uu and ≺\prec.

Lemma 2.1.4.
  • (1)

    Given I⊂𝒞I\subset\mathcal{C}, if GG is a ≺u\prec_{u}-standard basis of II then inu​(G)\mathrm{in}_{u}(G) is a (homogeneous) standard basis of inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I) for ≺\prec.

  • (2)

    Exp≺u(I)=Exp≺(inu(I))\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec_{u}}(I)=\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(I)).

Proof.

Statement (2) easily follows from (1) and the fact that for any g∈Gg\in G, exp≺u(g)=exp≺(inu(g))\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g)=\exp_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g)). Let us prove (1). Let f′f^{\prime} be in inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I). We want to prove that exp≺⁡(f′)\exp_{\prec}(f^{\prime}) is in exp≺⁡(inu​(g))+ℕn\exp_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g))+\mathbb{N}^{n} for some g∈Gg\in G. By considering the homogeneous part of f′f^{\prime} that contains the ≺\prec-leading term, we may assume f′f^{\prime} to be homogeneous. Let f∈If\in I be such that inu​(f)=f′\mathrm{in}_{u}(f)=f^{\prime} and let us consider the division of ff by GG w.r.t. ≺u\prec_{u} as in Theorem 2.1.2: f=∑1rqj​gjf=\sum_{1}^{r}q_{j}g_{j} where G={g1,…,gr}G=\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\} with

(⋆)Supp(qj)+exp≺u(gj)⊂Δj.(\star)\qquad\mathrm{Supp}(q_{j})+\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g_{j})\subset\Delta_{j}.

We have ordu​(f)≥ordu​(qj​gj)\mathrm{ord}^{u}(f)\geq\mathrm{ord}^{u}(q_{j}g_{j}) for any jj. Let qj′=inu​(qj)q^{\prime}_{j}=\mathrm{in}_{u}(q_{j}) if ordu​(f)=ordu​(qj​gj)\mathrm{ord}^{u}(f)=\mathrm{ord}^{u}(q_{j}g_{j}) and qj′=0q^{\prime}_{j}=0 otherwise then f′=∑1rqj′​inu​(gj)f^{\prime}=\sum_{1}^{r}q^{\prime}_{j}\mathrm{in}_{u}(g_{j}). Since exp≺u(g)=exp≺(inu(g))\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g)=\exp_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g)), the partition of ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n} associated with the exp≺u(gj)\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g_{j}) is the same as that associated with exp≺⁡(inu​(gj))\exp_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g_{j})). Moreover, for any h∈𝒞h\in\mathcal{C}, Supp⁡(inu​(h))⊂Supp⁡(h)\mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(h))\subset\mathrm{Supp}(h), thus the relation (⋆)(\star) becomes

Supp⁡(qj′)+exp≺⁡(inu​(gj))⊂Δj.\mathrm{Supp}(q^{\prime}_{j})+\exp_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g_{j}))\subset\Delta_{j}.

This means that the remainder of the division of f′f^{\prime} by the inu​(gj)\mathrm{in}_{u}(g_{j}) w.r.t. ≺\prec is zero from which the conclusion follows. ∎

Now given a standard basis GG of J⊂gru​(𝒞)J\subset\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}). We say that GG is minimal if for g,g′∈Gg,g^{\prime}\in G, exp≺⁡(g)∈exp≺⁡(g′)+ℕn\exp_{\prec}(g)\in\exp_{\prec}(g^{\prime})+\mathbb{N}^{n} implies g=g′g=g^{\prime}. We say that GG is reduced if it is minimal, unitary (i.e. lc≺​(g)=1\mathrm{lc}_{\prec}(g)=1 for any g∈Gg\in G) and if for any g∈Gg\in G, Supp⁡(g)∖{exp≺⁡(g)}⊂ℕn∖Exp≺​(I)\mathrm{Supp}(g)\smallsetminus\{\exp_{\prec}(g)\}\subset\mathbb{N}^{n}\smallsetminus\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec}(I).

Lemma 2.1.5.
  • (1)

    Given a homogeneous ideal JJ in gru​(𝒞)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}) and a local order ≺\prec, a reduced standard basis w.r.t. ≺\prec exists and is unique. Moreover it is made of homogeneous elements.

  • (2)

    Given II in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, if GG is the reduced ≺u\prec_{u}-standard basis then inu​(G)\mathrm{in}_{u}(G) is the reduced ≺\prec-standard basis of inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I).

Proof.

The proof of the first statement is classical, we omit it. The second one easily follows from the fact that for any g∈Gg\in G, exp≺u(g)=exp≺(inu(g))\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g)=\exp_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g)) and Supp⁡(inu​(g))⊂Supp⁡(g)\mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g))\subset\mathrm{Supp}(g). ∎

Lemma 2.1.6.

Suppose we have two local orders ≺1\prec_{1} and ≺2\prec_{2} and a homogeneous ideal J⊂gru​(𝒞)J\subset\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{C}). Let GG be a (resp. the reduced) ≺1\prec_{1}-standard basis of JJ and suppose for any g∈Gg\in G that exp≺1(g)=exp≺2(g)\exp_{\prec_{1}}(g)=\exp_{\prec_{2}}(g) then GG is a (resp. the reduced) ≺2\prec_{2}-standard basis of JJ.

Sketch of Proof.

Let f∈Jf\in J. Divide ff by GG w.r.t ≺1\prec_{1} for which the remainder is zero. By assumption, this division is also the division w.r.t ≺2\prec_{2}, and since the remainder is zero, GG is a ≺2\prec_{2}-standard basis of JJ. The statement concerning the reducibility is trivial. ∎

2.2. Back to Gröbner fans

For a local weight vector u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}, call supp⁡(u)={1≤i≤n|ui≠0}\mathrm{supp}(u)=\{1\leq i\leq n|u_{i}\neq 0\} the support of uu. By lemma 2.1.1, we have:

u′∈S𝒞​(u)⇔supp⁡(u)=supp⁡(u′).u^{\prime}\in S_{\mathcal{C}}(u)\iff\mathrm{supp}(u)=\mathrm{supp}(u^{\prime}).
Proposition 2.2.1.

Given an ideal II in 𝒞\mathcal{C} and u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}, then for any local order ≺\prec, the ≺u\prec_{u}-reduced standard basis GG of II satisfies:

CI[u]={u′∈𝒰loc|supp(u)=supp(u′) and ∀g∈G,inu(g)=inu′(g)}.C_{I}[u]=\{u^{\prime}\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}|\mathrm{supp}(u)=\mathrm{supp}(u^{\prime})\textrm{ and }\forall g\in G,\mathrm{in}_{u}(g)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g)\}.
Proof.

We already know that u′∈S𝒞​(u)⇔supp⁡(u)=supp⁡(u′)u^{\prime}\in S_{\mathcal{C}}(u)\iff\mathrm{supp}(u)=\mathrm{supp}(u^{\prime}) then under this assumption we have to prove that inu​(g)=inu′​(g)\mathrm{in}_{u}(g)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g) for any g∈Gg\in G if and only if inu​(I)=inu′​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(I). Take u′u^{\prime} in the RHS. By assumption, for any g∈Gg\in G, exp≺u(g)=exp≺(inu(g))=exp≺(inu′(g))=exp≺u′(g)\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g)=\exp_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g))=\exp_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g))=\exp_{\prec_{u^{\prime}}}(g) so by lemma 2.1.6, GG is also the ≺u′\prec_{u^{\prime}}-reduced standard basis of II. It follows that inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I) and inu′​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(I) have a common set of generators which is inu​(G)=inu′​(G)\mathrm{in}_{u}(G)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(G).

Now take u′u^{\prime} in the LHS. By Lemma 2.1.4(2), we have Exp≺u(I)=Exp≺(inu(I))=Exp≺(inu′(I))=Exp≺u′(I)\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec_{u}}(I)=\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(I))=\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(I))=\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec_{u^{\prime}}}(I) which implies that GG is the reduced standard basis for ≺u′\prec_{u^{\prime}}. Thus by lemma 2.1.5(2), inu​(G)\mathrm{in}_{u}(G) and inu′​(G)\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(G) are both the ≺\prec-reduced standard basis of inu​(I)=inu′​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(I). By unicity of the reduced standard basis, inu​(G)=inu′​(G)\mathrm{in}_{u}(G)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(G). As a consequence, u′∈u^{\prime}\in RHS. ∎

Corollary 2.2.2.

Let II be an ideal in 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0} and let I^=O^⋅I\hat{I}={\hat{O}}\cdot I then the Gröbner fans ℰ⁡(I,𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) and ℰ⁡(I^,𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}(\hat{I},\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) are equal.

Proof.

Let uu be in 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}. Let GG be the ≺u\prec_{u}-reduced standard basis of II then by using the Buchberger criterion involving the SS-functions (see [CG04, Prop. 1.6.2]), we obtain that GG is a ≺u\prec_{u}-standard basis of I^\hat{I} which in turn implies that it is the reduced one. Moreover by lemma 2.1.1, we have that SO^​(u)=S𝒪0​(u)S_{{\hat{O}}}(u)=S_{\mathcal{O}_{0}}(u) thus CI​[u]=CI^​[u]C_{I}[u]=C_{\hat{I}}[u] which completes the proof. ∎

With this corollary, we may assume that our ideal is in O^{\hat{O}}. We will work in O^{\hat{O}} for the rest of this section. Let gg be in O^{\hat{O}}, we define its Newton polyhedron as the following convex hull:

New⁡(g)=conv⁡(Supp⁡(g)+ℕn).\mathrm{New}(g)=\mathrm{conv}(\mathrm{Supp}(g)+\mathbb{N}^{n}).

The set Supp⁡(g)+ℕn\mathrm{Supp}(g)+\mathbb{N}^{n} is by definition stable by sums so let E⁡(g)E(g) be the minimal finite subset of Supp⁡(g)\mathrm{Supp}(g) such that Supp⁡(g)+ℕn=E⁡(g)+ℕn\mathrm{Supp}(g)+\mathbb{N}^{n}=E(g)+\mathbb{N}^{n}. As a consequence we have

New⁡(g)=conv⁡(E⁡(g))+ℝ≥0n\mathrm{New}(g)=\mathrm{conv}(E(g))+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}

which implies that New⁡(g)\mathrm{New}(g) is strictly speaking a polyhedron [Zi95, p. 30].

First we have the following result which is a part of Theorem 2.0.1.

Theorem 2.2.3.

For any ideal II in O^{\hat{O}}, the set {inu​(I)|u∈𝒰loc}\{\mathrm{in}_{u}(I)|u\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}\} is finite.

Proof.

We sketch the proof by giving the main steps since it is very similar to that of [ACG01, Th. 4].

  • (a)

    Given g∈O^g\in{\hat{O}}, the set of exp≺⁡(g)\exp_{\prec}(g), ≺\prec being any local order, is finite. By using the same arguments as in the proof of [ACG01, Prop. 17], we can easily show that it is contained in E⁡(g)E(g).

  • (a’)

    The set of inu​(g)\mathrm{in}_{u}(g), u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}, is finite. Indeed it is in one to one correspondence with the set of faces of New⁡(g)\mathrm{New}(g).

  • (b)

    Given an ideal II in O^{\hat{O}}, the set {Exp≺​(I)|≺ is a local order}\{\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec}(I)|\prec\textrm{ is a local order}\} is finite. The proof uses the same arguments as that of [ACG01, Th. 5] and is based on (a). We can also prove it as [St95, Th. 1.2].

  • (c)

    This last step is the main part. Thanks to the preceding statement, it is enough to prove the following: Given E=Exp≺​(I)E=\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec}(I) for some local order ≺\prec, the set of all inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I) such that Exp≺u(I)=E\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec_{u}}(I)=E is finite. Let GG be a ≺\prec-standard basis of II then for any uu as above, inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I) is generated by the set {inu​(g)|g∈G}\{\mathrm{in}_{u}(g)|g\in G\}. By (a’), there is only a finite number of such sets.

∎

Now let uu be in 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} and let ≺\prec be any local order. Let GG be the ≺u\prec_{u}-reduced standard basis of II. Let

be the Minkowski sum of the Newton polyhedra of the gg in GG.

Proposition 2.2.4.
CI​[u]=NQ​(faceu​(Q))C_{I}[u]=\mathrm{N}_{Q}(\mathrm{face}_{u}(Q))

where NQ​(faceu​(⋅))\mathrm{N}_{Q}(\mathrm{face}_{u}(\cdot)) denotes the normal cone of the face w.r.t. uu.

As a direct consequence:

Corollary 2.2.5.

The Gröbner cone CI​[u]C_{I}[u] is a convex rational relatively open polyhedral cone.

The proof of the proposition will be decomposed into several lemmas.

For g∈O^g\in{\hat{O}} and u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}, let Eu​(g)E_{u}(g) be the elements of E⁡(g)E(g) which are maximum for the scalar product with uu. Let ei∈ℕne_{i}\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n be the canonical base of the semi-group ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}.

Lemma 2.2.6.
faceu​(New⁡(g))=conv⁡(Eu​(g))+∑i∉supp⁡(u)ℝ≥0⋅ei.\mathrm{face}_{u}(\mathrm{New}(g))=\mathrm{conv}(E_{u}(g))+\sum_{i\notin\mathrm{supp}(u)}\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\cdot e_{i}.
Proof.

It is easy to see that faceu​(ℝ≥0n)\mathrm{face}_{u}(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}) is equal to the second member of the RHS. Moreover there is a general identity for polyhedra

faceu​(P+P′)=faceu​(P)+faceu​(P′).\mathrm{face}_{u}(P+P^{\prime})=\mathrm{face}_{u}(P)+\mathrm{face}_{u}(P^{\prime}).

Thus it suffices to show this equality: faceu​(conv⁡(E⁡(g)))=conv⁡(Eu​(g))\mathrm{face}_{u}(\mathrm{conv}(E(g)))=\mathrm{conv}(E_{u}(g)). Let us prove it. Take α\alpha in the LHS. Written as a sum α=∑jcj​αj\alpha=\sum_{j}c_{j}\alpha_{j}, cj≥0c_{j}\geq 0, ∑jcj=1\sum_{j}c_{j}=1, of elements in E⁡(g)E(g), we see that the scalar product u⋅αu\cdot\alpha is equal to some u⋅αju\cdot\alpha_{j}. This implies that uu evaluated on the LHS or on the RHS gives the same number. From this observation, we easily derive the desired equality. ∎

Let g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} be in O^{\hat{O}}. Put Qj=New⁡(gj)Q_{j}=\mathrm{New}(g_{j}) and let QQ be the Minkowski sum of the QjQ_{j}’s.

For any u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}, we have

This lemma is known for polytopes (see [Zi95], Prop. 7.12, p. 198). We can prove it by reducing the case of polyhedra to the case of polytopes by truncating our polyhedra.

Now, here is the last lemma before the proof of proposition 2.2.4.

Lemma 2.2.8.

Let g∈O^g\in{\hat{O}} then for u,u′∈𝒰locu,u^{\prime}\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}:

[inu(g)=inu′(g) and supp(u)=supp(u′)]⇔faceu(New(g))=faceu′(New(g)).\big[\mathrm{in}_{u}(g)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g)\textrm{ and }\mathrm{supp}(u)=\mathrm{supp}(u^{\prime})\big]\iff\mathrm{face}_{u}(\mathrm{New}(g))=\mathrm{face}_{u^{\prime}}(\mathrm{New}(g)).
Proof.

First let us prove this claim:
Claim. Under the condition supp⁡(u)=supp⁡(u′)\mathrm{supp}(u)=\mathrm{supp}(u^{\prime}) the following equivalence holds: Eu​(g)=Eu′​(g)⇔inu​(g)=inu′​(g)E_{u}(g)=E_{u^{\prime}}(g)\iff\mathrm{in}_{u}(g)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g).
Suppose we have Eu​(g)=Eu′​(g)E_{u}(g)=E_{u^{\prime}}(g), it is enough to prove Supp⁡(inu​(g))=Supp⁡(inu′​(g))\mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g))=\mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g)). Let α\alpha be in Supp​(inu​(g))\mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{in}_{u}(g)). Then there exists e∈E⁡(g)e\in E(g) and α′∈ℕn\alpha^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}^{n} such that α=e+α′\alpha=e+\alpha^{\prime}. We have u⋅α≤u⋅eu\cdot\alpha\leq u\cdot e but by definition of inu​(g)\mathrm{in}_{u}(g), u⋅α≥u⋅eu\cdot\alpha\geq u\cdot e. Thus ee belongs to EuE_{u} which is equal to Eu′​(g)E_{u^{\prime}}(g) by assumption. This also means that u⋅α′=0u\cdot\alpha^{\prime}=0 but since supp⁡(u)=supp⁡(u′)\mathrm{supp}(u)=\mathrm{supp}(u^{\prime}), this implies u′⋅α′=0u^{\prime}\cdot\alpha^{\prime}=0. Thus u′⋅α=u′⋅eu^{\prime}\cdot\alpha=u^{\prime}\cdot e. Now take any α′′\alpha^{\prime\prime} in Supp⁡(g)\mathrm{Supp}(g). We can write α′′=e′+a′\alpha^{\prime\prime}=e^{\prime}+a^{\prime} with e′∈Ee^{\prime}\in E and a′∈ℕna^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}^{n}. Therefore, u′⋅α′′≤u′⋅e′≤u′⋅e=u′⋅αu^{\prime}\cdot\alpha^{\prime\prime}\leq u^{\prime}\cdot e^{\prime}\leq u^{\prime}\cdot e=u^{\prime}\cdot\alpha. This means that α\alpha belongs to Supp​(inu′​(g))\mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g)). By symmetry the other inclusion holds. The right-left implication can be shown with similar arguments.

Let us return to the proof of the lemma. The left-right implication follows immediately from the claim and Lemma 2.2.6. For the right-left one, by using the same arguments as in the proof of the previous lemma (i.e. the boundedness of conv⁡(E)\mathrm{conv}(E)), we can show that supp⁡(u)=supp⁡(u′)\mathrm{supp}(u)=\mathrm{supp}(u^{\prime}) and Eu​(g)=Eu′​(g)E_{u}(g)=E_{u^{\prime}}(g), we then conclude by the claim above. ∎

Now we are ready to give the

Proof of Proposition 2.2.4.

By lemma 2.2.7,

NQ​(faceu​(Q))=⋂j=1rNNew⁡(gj)​(faceu​(New⁡(gj))).\mathrm{N}_{Q}(\mathrm{face}_{u}(Q))=\bigcap_{j=1}^{r}\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{New}(g_{j})}(\mathrm{face}_{u}(\mathrm{New}(g_{j}))).

By the previous lemma,

NNew⁡(gj)​(faceu​(New⁡(gj)))={u′∈S⁡(u)|inu​(gj)=inu′​(gj)}.\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{New}(g_{j})}(\mathrm{face}_{u}(\mathrm{New}(g_{j})))=\{u^{\prime}\in S(u)|\mathrm{in}_{u}(g_{j})=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g_{j})\}.

We then conclude by using Prop. 2.2.1. ∎

2.3. Proof of Theorem 2.0.1

We recall that we are given an ideal II in O^{\hat{O}}. Let u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

Lemma 2.3.1.

For any u′∈CI​[u]¯∖CI​[u]u^{\prime}\in\overline{C_{I}[u]}\smallsetminus C_{I}[u] there exists a local order ≺\prec such that the reduced standard bases of II with respect to ≺u\prec_{u} and to ≺u′\prec_{u^{\prime}} are the same.

Proof.

The proof is inspired by [Ba05, Prop. 2.1]. We define the order ≺\prec in a lexicographical way by uu and by any local order <<. Note that ≺=≺u\prec=\prec_{u}. Let GG be the ≺\prec-reduced standard basis of II. In order to prove the lemma, it is enough (see lemma 2.1.6) to show the following for any g∈Gg\in G: exp≺u(g)=exp≺u′(g)\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g)=\exp_{\prec_{u^{\prime}}}(g).

exp≺u′(g)\displaystyle\exp_{\prec_{u^{\prime}}}(g) =\displaystyle= exp≺u′(inu′(g))\displaystyle\exp_{\prec_{u^{\prime}}}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g))
=\displaystyle= exp≺u(inu′(g)) by definition of ≺.\displaystyle\exp_{\prec_{u}}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g))\textrm{ by definition of }\prec.

To finish it remains to prove this claim: exp≺u(inu′(g))=exp≺u(g)\exp_{\prec_{u}}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g))=\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g).
First since Supp⁡(inu′​(g))⊂Supp⁡(g)\mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g))\subset\mathrm{Supp}(g), we have exp≺u(g)⪰uexp≺u(inu′(g))\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g)\succeq_{u}\exp_{\prec_{u}}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g)). Let us prove the reverse inequality. First we prove:

(⋆)ordu′(g)=u′⋅exp≺u(g).(\star)\qquad\mathrm{ord}^{u^{\prime}}(g)=u^{\prime}\cdot\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g).

For any α∈Supp⁡(g)\alpha\in\mathrm{Supp}(g), and for any u′′∈CI​[u]u^{\prime\prime}\in C_{I}[u], u′′⋅exp≺u(g)≥u′′⋅αu^{\prime\prime}\cdot\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g)\geq u^{\prime\prime}\cdot\alpha. Since u′u^{\prime} is the limit of elements u′′∈CI​[u]u^{\prime\prime}\in C_{I}[u], we obtain the same inequality for u′u^{\prime} which proves (⋆)(\star). Therefore exp≺u(g)∈Supp(inu′(g))\exp_{\prec_{u}}(g)\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g)). The desired inequality is then a direct consequence of the definition of exp≺u(inu′(g))\exp_{\prec_{u}}(\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g)). The claim and the lemma are proven. ∎

Finally, we can prove Theorem 2.0.1.

Proof.

The proof is exactly the same as that of [St95, Prop. 2.4]. For the sake of completeness let us give the main arguments. For u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}, let u′u^{\prime} be in CI​[u]¯∖CI​[u]\overline{C_{I}[u]}\smallsetminus C_{I}[u]. Take an order ≺\prec as in the previous lemma and let GG be the ≺u\prec_{u}-reduced standard basis of II. Then by Prop. 2.2.4, CI​[u]=NQ​(faceu​(Q))C_{I}[u]=\mathrm{N}_{Q}(\mathrm{face}_{u}(Q)) and CI​[u′]=NQ​(faceu′​(Q))C_{I}[u^{\prime}]=\mathrm{N}_{Q}(\mathrm{face}_{u^{\prime}}(Q)) where QQ is the Minkowski sum of New⁡(g)\mathrm{New}(g) for g∈Gg\in G. By hypothesis on u′u^{\prime}, faceu​(Q)\mathrm{face}_{u}(Q) is a face of the polyhedron faceu′​(Q)\mathrm{face}_{u^{\prime}}(Q) thus CI​[u′]¯\overline{C_{I}[u^{\prime}]} is a face of the closed convex cone CI​[u]¯\overline{C_{I}[u]}.

Now let us check the two axioms for being a fan. For axiom (1), let FF be a face of the closure of some CI​[u]C_{I}[u]. Take any u′u^{\prime} in the relative interior of FF then by the arguments above, FF is equal to the face CI​[u′]¯\overline{C_{I}[u^{\prime}]}. For axiom (2), let u,u′u,u^{\prime} be any in 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} and consider the closed convex cone P=CI​[u]¯∩CI​[u′]¯P=\overline{C_{I}[u]}\cap\overline{C_{I}[u^{\prime}]}. We have seen that for any u′′∈Pu^{\prime\prime}\in P, CI​[u′′]¯\overline{C_{I}[u^{\prime\prime}]} is a face of both CI​[u]¯\overline{C_{I}[u]} and CI​[u′]¯\overline{C_{I}[u^{\prime}]}. Thus PP is a (finite) union of common faces. By convexity of PP this union is a singleton. ∎

Lemma 3.1.4.

For w=(u,v)w=(u,v), let us assume (for simplicity) that:

    ui<0u_{i}<0 for 1≤i≤n21\leq i\leq n_{2} with ui+vi=0u_{i}+v_{i}=0 for 1≤i≤n11\leq i\leq n_{1} and ui+vi>0u_{i}+v_{i}>0 for n1<i≤n2n_{1}<i\leq n_{2},

where ξi\xi_{i} is a commutative variable and for a⁡(x)∈𝐤⁡[[xn2+1,…,xn]]​[x1,…,xn2]a(x)\in{\bf k}[[x_{n_{2}+1},\ldots,x_{n}]][x_{1},\ldots,x_{n_{2}}], [∂i,a(x)]=∂a⁡(x)∂xi⋅h[\partial_{i},a(x)]=\frac{\partial a(x)}{\partial x_{i}}\cdot h. Concerning grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0})), we have the same result replacing 𝐤⁡[[xn2+1,…,xn]]\mathbf{k}[[x_{n_{2}+1},\ldots,x_{n}]] with ℂ⁡{xn2+1,…,xn}\mathbb{C}\{x_{n_{2}+1},\ldots,x_{n}\}.

Proof.

The proof consists of a simple verification. ∎

Let ww be in 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}. Given an admissible order ≺\prec, we define the (admissible) order ≺w\prec_{w} by refining the partial order defined by ww.

The ring grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})) is a bi-graded ring. There is a graduation by the total degree in the ∂i\partial_{i}, ξi\xi_{i} and hh. There is another graduation associated with ww. So in order to avoid confusions, a homogeneous element for the second graduation shall be called ww-homogeneous.

For any bihomogeneous P∈grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^))P\in\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})), there exists a unique (Q1,…,Qr,R)∈(grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)))r+1(Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{r},R)\in(\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})))^{r+1} made of bihomogeneous elements such that

    for any jj, if Qj≠0Q_{j}\neq 0 then Supp(Qj)+exp≺h(Pi)⊂Δj\mathrm{Supp}(Q_{j})+\exp_{\prec^{h}}(P_{i})\subset\Delta_{j}

  • •

    if R≠0R\neq 0, Supp⁡(R)⊂Δ¯\mathrm{Supp}(R)\subset\bar{\Delta}.

The division theorem in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}) is a particular case of the latter if we take w=(0)w=(0).

Moreover for any Q∈h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)Q\in h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}), Supp⁡(inw​(Q))⊂Supp⁡(Q)\mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{in}_{w}(Q))\subset\mathrm{Supp}(Q) so the relation (⋆′)(\star^{\prime}) becomes

3.2. Standard bases in the graded ring grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}))

The symbol ≺\prec still denotes any admissible order. Let JJ be a bihomogeneous ideal in grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})) or in grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0})) (and in the latter case, we take ≺=⊲\prec=\lhd). We define

Exp≺h(J)={exp≺h(f)|0≠f∈J}.\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec^{h}}(J)=\{\exp_{\prec^{h}}(f)|0\neq f\in J\}.

This set is stable by sums in 𝐍2​n+1{\bf N}^{2n+1}, thus by Dickson lemma:

Definition 3.2.1.

There exists a finite set G={g1,…,gr}⊂JG=\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\}\subset J such that

Exp≺h(J)=⋃j=1r(exp≺h(gj)+𝐍2​n+1).\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec^{h}}(J)=\bigcup_{j=1}^{r}(\exp_{\prec^{h}}(g_{j})+{\bf N}^{2n+1}).

Such a set is called a ≺h\prec^{h}-standard basis of JJ.

Given G⊂JG\subset J, the following statements are equivalent:

  • •

    GG is a bihomogeneous ≺h\prec^{h}-standard basis of JJ.

  • •

    For any f∈grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^))f\in\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})), f∈Jf\in J if and only if the remainder of the division of ff by GG (w.r.t. ≺h\prec^{h}) is zero.

In the following lemma, we gather the results needed in the sequel. The generalizations of the division theorem in the previous subsection are used to prove the following analogous statements with Lemmas 2.1.4, 2.1.5, 2.1.6.

Lemma 3.2.2.
  • •

    Given a bihomogeneous ideal JJ in grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})) (resp. in grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0}))) and an admissible order ≺\prec (resp. ≺=⊲\prec=\lhd), a reduced standard basis w.r.t. ≺h\prec^{h} exists and is unique. Moreover it is bihomogeneous.

    Let ≺1\prec_{1}, ≺2\prec_{2} be admissible orders. If GG is a homogeneous (the reduced) ≺1h\prec_{1}^{h}-standard basis of JJ and exp≺1h(g)=exp≺2h(g)\exp_{\prec_{1}^{h}}(g)=\exp_{\prec_{2}^{h}}(g) for any g∈Gg\in G then GG is a homogeneous (the reduced) ≺1h\prec_{1}^{h}-standard basis of JJ.

    Given II homogeneous in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}) (resp. h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0})), if GG is the reduced ≺wh\prec_{w}^{h}-standard basis of II then inw​(G)\mathrm{in}_{w}(G) is the reduced ≺h\prec^{h}-standard basis of inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(I). Moreover we have Exp≺wh(I)=Exp≺h(inw(I))\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec_{w}^{h}}(I)=\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec^{h}}(\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)).

After this corollary, we will work in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}) for the rest of the section.

Let us denote by π\pi the natural projection ℕ2​n×ℕ→ℕ2​n\mathbb{N}^{2n}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}^{2n}, (α,β,k)↦(α,β)(\alpha,\beta,k)\mapsto(\alpha,\beta). For g∈h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)g\in h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}) let us define the Newton polyhedron of gg as the following convex hull:

If we denote by 𝒲loc∗\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{*} the polar dual cone of 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}} then the set under bracket is 𝒲loc∗∩ℤ2​n\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{*}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2n}. 𝒲loc∗={∑i=1nλiei+∑i=1nλi′ei′|λi,λi′≥0}.\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{*}=\big\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}e_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda^{\prime}_{i}e^{\prime}_{i}|\ \lambda_{i},\lambda^{\prime}_{i}\geq 0\big\}.

Let E⁡(g)⊂π⁡(Supp⁡(g))E(g)\subset\pi(\mathrm{Supp}(g)) be a finite subset such that: π(Supp(g))+((⊕1nℕei)×(⊕1nℕei′))=E(g)+((⊕1nℕei)×(⊕1nℕei′))\pi(\mathrm{Supp}(g))+((\oplus_{1}^{n}\mathbb{N}e_{i})\times(\oplus_{1}^{n}\mathbb{N}e^{\prime}_{i}))=E(g)+((\oplus_{1}^{n}\mathbb{N}e_{i})\times(\oplus_{1}^{n}\mathbb{N}e^{\prime}_{i})). (3) New⁡(g)=conv⁡(E⁡(g))+𝒲loc∗,\mathrm{New}(g)=\mathrm{conv}(E(g))+\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{*},

which assures that New⁡(g)\mathrm{New}(g) is strictly speaking a polyhedron.

Let ww be in 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}, ≺\prec be any admissible order and GG be the ≺wh\prec_{w}^{h}-reduced standard basis of II. Let

CI​[w]=NQ​(facew​(Q))C_{I}[w]=\mathrm{N}_{Q}(\mathrm{face}_{w}(Q))

where NQ​(facew​(⋅))\mathrm{N}_{Q}(\mathrm{face}_{w}(\cdot)) denotes the normal cone of the face w.r.t. ww.

The proof will be based on the following lemmas.

Lemma 3.3.4.

For g∈h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)g\in h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}) and w∈𝒲locw\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}, let Ew​(g)E_{w}(g) be the set of elements in E⁡(g)E(g) which are maximum for the scalar product with ww then

(4) facew(New(g))=conv(Ew(g))+{∑i∉M⁡(w)λiei+∑i∉P⁡(w)λi′ei′|λi,λi′≥0}.\mathrm{face}_{w}(\mathrm{New}(g))=\mathrm{conv}(E_{w}(g))+\big\{\sum_{i\notin M(w)}\lambda_{i}e_{i}+\sum_{i\notin P(w)}\lambda^{\prime}_{i}e^{\prime}_{i}|\ \lambda_{i},\lambda^{\prime}_{i}\geq 0\big\}.

[inw(g)=inw′(g) and S(w)=S(w′)]⇔facew(New(g))=facew′(New(g)).\big[\mathrm{in}_{w}(g)=\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(g)\textrm{ and }S(w)=S(w^{\prime})\big]\iff\mathrm{face}_{w}(\mathrm{New}(g))=\mathrm{face}_{w^{\prime}}(\mathrm{New}(g)).

3.4. Proof of Theorem 3.0.1

Let II be a homogeneous ideal in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}).

Lemma 3.4.1.

Let w′∈CI​[w]¯∖CI​[w]w^{\prime}\in\overline{C_{I}[w]}\setminus C_{I}[w] for some w∈𝒲locw\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}. Then there exists an admissible order ≺\prec such that the reduced standard bases of II w.r.t. ≺wh\prec_{w}^{h} and to ≺w′h\prec_{w^{\prime}}^{h} agree.

Proof.

The proof is a slight modification of [Ba05, Prop. 2.1]. Since it is similar to that of lemma 2.3.1, we sketch it. We define the order ≺\prec first by ww and then by any admissible order <<. Let GG be the ≺h\prec^{h}-reduced standard basis of II. Note that for homogeneous elements, exp≺h\exp_{\prec^{h}} coincides with exp≺wh\exp_{\prec_{w}^{h}}. Now, to prove the lemma, it is enough to show the following for any g∈Gg\in G: exp≺wh(g)=exp≺w′h(g)\exp_{\prec_{w}^{h}}(g)=\exp_{\prec_{w^{\prime}}^{h}}(g).

exp≺w′h(g)\displaystyle\exp_{\prec_{w^{\prime}}^{h}}(g) =\displaystyle= exp≺w′h(inw′(g)) because g is homogeneous\displaystyle\exp_{\prec_{w^{\prime}}^{h}}(\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(g))\textrm{ because }g\textrm{ is homogeneous}
=\displaystyle= exp≺wh(inw′(g)) by definition of ≺\displaystyle\exp_{\prec_{w}^{h}}(\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(g))\textrm{ by definition of }\prec
=\displaystyle= exp≺wh(g).\displaystyle\exp_{\prec_{w}^{h}}(g).

The last equality can be proved as in the proof of lemma 2.3.1. ∎

By [ACG01, Th. 4], we know that the number of different inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(I) is finite, so in order to finish the proof of Theorem 3.0.1 it remains to prove that ℰ¯​(I,𝒲loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) satisfies the two axioms for being a complex which can be done with the same arguments as in the proof of Theorem 2.0.1.

When considering applications or when doing calculations, we often need to consider Gröbner fans restricted to linear subspaces in the space of the weight vectors.

Corollary 3.4.2.

Let LL be a linear subspace in ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n} then for any homogeneous ideal II in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}), the restriction of ℰ¯​(I,𝒲loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) to LL is a polyhedral fan in 𝒲loc∩L\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L.

Proof.

Since we have proved that the local Gröbner fan is a polyhedral fan, the restriction is also a polyhedral fan [Zi95, p. 195]. ∎

4. Existence and comparison of the different Gröbner fans

In what follows, we will discuss about the relation between the several kinds of Gröbner fans. We will discuss both for polynomial rings and associate rings and the case of differential operators.

Proofs are analogous each other. However statements are different because the spaces of the weight vectors are different.

In order to clarify the difference, we present lemmas and propositions for all the cases. The proofs will be made for the case of differential rings.

In the following 𝒰loc′\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime} denotes the u∈𝒰locu\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} such that ui<0u_{i}<0 and 𝒲loc′\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime} denotes the w=(u,v)∈𝒲locw=(u,v)\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}} with ui<0u_{i}<0 and ui+vi>0u_{i}+v_{i}>0. In other terms, 𝒰loc′\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime} and 𝒲loc′\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime} are the interior of 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} and 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}} respectively.

4.1. Without homogenization

4.1.1. The local Gröbner fan

In order to compare the Gröbner fans, let us deal with the graded algebras first.

Let uu be in 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} and w=(u,v)w={(u,v)} be in 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}. Let us take the same situation as above, then:

Corollary 4.1.3.

For any u∈𝒰loc′u\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime}, gru​(O^)=gru​(𝒪0)=gru​(𝐤​[x]0)=gru​(𝐤⁡[x])\mathrm{gr}^{u}({\hat{O}})=\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathcal{O}_{0})=\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0})=\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathbf{k}[x]). For any w∈𝒲loc′w\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime}, we have grw​(D^)=grw​(𝒟0)=grw​(D{0})=grw​(D)\mathrm{gr}^{w}(\hat{D})=\mathrm{gr}^{w}(\mathcal{D}_{0})=\mathrm{gr}^{w}(D_{\{0\}})=\mathrm{gr}^{w}(D).

Proof of the Lemma.

For statement (1), the equality is trivial since grw​(D)\mathrm{gr}^{w}(D) is canonically isomorphic to 𝐤[x1,…,xn,ξn1+1,…,ξn3,∂1,…,∂n1,∂n3+1,…,∂n]\mathbf{k}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\xi_{n_{1}+1},\ldots,\xi_{n_{3}},\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n_{1}},\partial_{n_{3}+1},\ldots,\partial_{n}].

Let us prove statement (2). First, let us remark that both rings in this statement are subrings of grw​(D^)\mathrm{gr}^{w}(\hat{D}) then it is enough to prove the double inclusion. For the left-right one, it is enough to show that inw​(P)\mathrm{in}_{w}(P) is in the RHS for any P∈D{0}P\in D_{\{0\}}. Such a PP is equal to 1/q⁡(x)​P′1/q(x)P^{\prime} with P′∈DP^{\prime}\in D and q⁡(x)∈𝐤⁡[x]q(x)\in\mathbf{k}[x] with q⁡(0)≠0q(0)\neq 0. Since inw​(1/q⁡(x)​P′)=inw​(1/q⁡(x))​inw​(P′)\mathrm{in}_{w}(1/q(x)P^{\prime})=\mathrm{in}_{w}(1/q(x))\mathrm{in}_{w}(P^{\prime}), let us show that inw​(1/q​(x))\mathrm{in}_{w}(1/q(x)) is in 𝐤​[x]⟨xn2+1,…,xn⟩\mathbf{k}[x]_{\langle x_{n_{2}+1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle}.

For simplicity, assume that q⁡(0)=1q(0)=1 and write q⁡(x)=1−v0−v1q(x)=1-v_{0}-v_{1} where v0=v0​(xn2+1,…,xn)v_{0}=v_{0}(x_{n_{2}+1},\ldots,x_{n}) and v1v_{1} is in the ideal generated by x1,…,xn2x_{1},\ldots,x_{n_{2}}. As a series in 𝐤⁡[[x]]\mathbf{k}[[x]], we have

1/q⁡(x)=V1+1+v0+v02+⋯1/q(x)=V_{1}+1+v_{0}+v_{0}^{2}+\cdots

where V1∈∑i=1n2𝐤⁡[[x]]​xiV_{1}\in\sum_{i=1}^{n_{2}}\mathbf{k}[[x]]x_{i}. By comparing the ww-orders, we see that 0=ordw​(1+v0+v02+⋯)>ordw​(V1)0=\mathrm{ord}_{w}(1+v_{0}+v_{0}^{2}+\cdots)>\mathrm{ord}_{w}(V_{1}). As a consequence inw​(1/q⁡(x))=1+v0+v02+⋯=1/(1−v0)\mathrm{in}_{w}(1/q(x))=1+v_{0}+v_{0}^{2}+\cdots=1/(1-v_{0}) and it is in 𝐤​[x]⟨xn2+1,…,xn⟩\mathbf{k}[x]_{\langle x_{n_{2}+1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle}.

The right-left inclusion follows from the following: for any PP in the RHS, PP is a finite sum of elements of the form 1/q⊗inw​(P′)1/q\otimes\mathrm{in}_{w}(P^{\prime}) where P′∈DP^{\prime}\in D and q∈𝐤⁡[xn2+1,…,xn]q\in\mathbf{k}[x_{n_{2}+1},\ldots,x_{n}] with q⁡(0)≠0q(0)\neq 0. But for such elements, we have inw​(1/q)=1/q\mathrm{in}_{w}(1/q)=1/q so inw​(1/q​P′)=1/q⋅inw​(P′)\mathrm{in}_{w}(1/qP^{\prime})=1/q\cdot\mathrm{in}_{w}(P^{\prime}) and then PP belongs to the LHS.

Finally, the proof of statement (3) uses the same arguments as that of (1) and (2). ∎

Our main goal in this part is to present an algorithm for computing two kinds of fan, the first one is the following.

Definition 4.1.4.

Let II be an ideal in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x] (resp. in DD). The set ℰ⁡(𝐤​[x]0​I,𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) (resp. ℰ⁡(D{0}​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(D_{\{0\}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})) shall be called the local (open) Gröbner fan of II (at 0∈𝐤n0\in\mathbf{k}^{n}).

Take u∈𝒰loc′u\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime} (resp. w∈𝒲loc′w\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime}). We have seen that in this case, all the graded rings that we considered are equal to gru​(𝐤​[x])\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathbf{k}[x]) (resp. grw​(D)\mathrm{gr}^{w}(D)), so the initial ideals considered in the next proposition are comparable.

Proposition 4.1.5.

Take u∈𝒰loc′u\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime} and w∈𝒲loc′w\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime}.

  • (i)

    If I⊂𝐤⁡[x]I\subset\mathbf{k}[x] then inu​(𝐤​[x]0​I)=inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I)=\mathrm{in}_{u}(I).

  • (ii)

    If I⊂𝐤​[x]0I\subset\mathbf{k}[x]_{0} then inu​(O^​I)=inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}({\hat{O}}I)=\mathrm{in}_{u}(I).

  • (iii)

    If 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C} and I⊂𝐤​[x]0I\subset\mathbf{k}[x]_{0} then inu​(𝒪0​I)=inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(\mathcal{O}_{0}I)=\mathrm{in}_{u}(I).

  • (iv)

    If 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C} and I⊂𝒪0I\subset\mathcal{O}_{0} then inu​(O^​I)=inu​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}({\hat{O}}I)=\mathrm{in}_{u}(I).

  • (1)

    If I⊂DI\subset D then inw​(D{0}​I)=inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(D_{\{0\}}I)=\mathrm{in}_{w}(I).

  • (2)

    If I⊂D{0}I\subset D_{\{0\}} then inw​(D^​I)=inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(\hat{D}I)=\mathrm{in}_{w}(I).

  • (3)

    If 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C} and I⊂D{0}I\subset D_{\{0\}} then inw​(𝒟0​I)=inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(\mathcal{D}_{0}I)=\mathrm{in}_{w}(I).

  • (4)

    If 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C} and I⊂𝒟0I\subset\mathcal{D}_{0} then inw​(D^​I)=inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(\hat{D}I)=\mathrm{in}_{w}(I).

Proof.

As we said, all these initial ideals are in a same ring grw​(D)\mathrm{gr}^{w}(D). Let us first suppose that II is in DD and let us prove that inw​(D^​I)=inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(\hat{D}I)=\mathrm{in}_{w}(I). Using the inclusions

inw​(I)⊂inw​(D{0}​I)(⊂inw​(𝒟0​I))⊂inw​(D^​I),\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)\subset\mathrm{in}_{w}(D_{\{0\}}I)(\subset\mathrm{in}_{w}(\mathcal{D}_{0}I))\subset\mathrm{in}_{w}(\hat{D}I),

claim (1) follows from the inclusion inw​(D^​I)⊂inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(\hat{D}I)\subset\mathrm{in}_{w}(I), that we shall subsequently prove.

For this inclusion, it is enough to prove that for P∈D^​IP\in\hat{D}I, inw​(P)∈inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(P)\in\mathrm{in}_{w}(I). Such a PP can be written as a finite sum

P=∑jcj​(x)​PjP=\sum_{j}c_{j}(x)P_{j}

with cj​(x)∈𝐤​[[x]]c_{j}(x)\in\mathbf{k}[[x]] and Pj∈IP_{j}\in I. Put m=ordw​(P)m=\mathrm{ord}_{w}(P) and for each jj, let us write cj​(x)=∑αcj,α​xαc_{j}(x)=\sum_{\alpha}c_{j,\alpha}x^{\alpha} where cj,α∈𝐤c_{j,\alpha}\in\mathbf{k}. Now let us decompose cj​(x)=pj​(x)+sj​(x)c_{j}(x)=p_{j}(x)+s_{j}(x) where

pj​(x)=∑u⋅α+ordw​(Pj)≥mcj,α​xα.p_{j}(x)=\sum_{u\cdot\alpha+\mathrm{ord}_{w}(P_{j})\geq m}c_{j,\alpha}x^{\alpha}.

Since all the uiu_{i} are negative, each pj​(x)p_{j}(x) is a polynomial. By construction, we have ordw​(sj​(x)​Pj)<m\mathrm{ord}_{w}(s_{j}(x)P_{j})<m. Therefore,

inw​(P)=inw​(∑jpj​(x)​Pj)∈inw​(I),\mathrm{in}_{w}(P)=\mathrm{in}_{w}\left(\sum_{j}p_{j}(x)P_{j}\right)\in\mathrm{in}_{w}(I),

and the inclusion is proved.

Finally, it is easy to remark that the method used for proving claim (1) can be adapted with few changes to prove the other claims. ∎

As a trivial consequence, we obtain:

Corollary 4.1.6.

For II in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x], ℰ⁡(I,𝒰loc′)=ℰ⁡(𝐤​[x]0​I,𝒰loc′)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime})=\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime}). For I⊂DI\subset D, ℰ⁡(I,𝒲loc′)=ℰ⁡(D{0}​I,𝒲loc′)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime})=\mathcal{E}(D_{\{0\}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime}).

In other words, if we restrict ourselves to the interior of the weight vector space then, global and local Gröbner fans do agree. So the obstruction to have equality should be found in the border and indeed they are not equal in general.

Example 4.1.7.
  1. (1)

    Take I=⟨1⟩I=\langle 1\rangle in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x]. Then ℰ⁡(O^​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}({\hat{O}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is equal to ℰ⁡(I,𝒲loc)∩SO^\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})\cap S_{\hat{O}} where SO^S_{\hat{O}} is the stratification given by the graded rings. After this example we may ask if such a relation always happens. We shall see in Th. 5.1.1 that this relation is true if the ideal II is homogeneous for a weight vector having positive components. In the general case, the relation does not hold:

  2. (2)

    Take I=⟨1−x3,x1+x2⟩I=\langle 1-x_{3},x_{1}+x_{2}\rangle in 𝐤⁡[x1,x2,x3]\mathbf{k}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}]. For the weights, we consider the space U12={(u1,u2,0)|ui≤0}U_{12}=\{(u_{1},u_{2},0)|u_{i}\leq 0\}. In this space, the open global Gröbner fan has three cones {u1<u2}\{u_{1}<u_{2}\}, {u1=u2}\{u_{1}=u_{2}\}, {u1>u2}\{u_{1}>u_{2}\} while the local Gröbner fan is trivial since 1−x31-x_{3} is invertible. Here trivial means that we have four cones {0},{u1<0,u2=0},{u1<0,u2<0},{u1=0,u2<0}\{0\},\{u_{1}<0,u_{2}=0\},\{u_{1}<0,u_{2}<0\},\{u_{1}=0,u_{2}<0\}. In this example, ℰ⁡(O^​I,U12)\mathcal{E}({\hat{O}}I,U_{12}) has 4 cones and ℰ⁡(I,U12)∩SO^\mathcal{E}(I,U_{12})\cap S_{\hat{O}} has 6 cones.

For a given algebraic ideal II, we called ℰ⁡(I,𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) (resp. in 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) the local Gröbner fan of II, let us precise this term.

Proposition 4.1.8.
  • (i)

    For I⊂𝐤​[x]0I\subset\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}, ℰ⁡(I,𝒰loc)=ℰ⁡(O^​I,𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}})=\mathcal{E}({\hat{O}}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

  • (ii)

    If 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C} and I⊂𝒪0I\subset\mathcal{O}_{0} then ℰ⁡(I,𝒰loc)=ℰ⁡(O^​I,𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}})=\mathcal{E}({\hat{O}}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

  • (1)

    For I⊂D{0}I\subset D_{\{0\}}, ℰ⁡(I,𝒲loc)=ℰ⁡(D^​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})=\mathcal{E}(\hat{D}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

  • (2)

    If 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C} and I⊂𝒟0I\subset\mathcal{D}_{0} then ℰ⁡(I,𝒲loc)=ℰ⁡(D^​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})=\mathcal{E}(\hat{D}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

This implies in particular that for a given II in DD, the following Gröbner fans do agree: ℰ⁡(D{0}​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(D_{\{0\}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}), ℰ⁡(𝒟0​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{D}_{0}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) (if 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C}), ℰ⁡(D^​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(\hat{D}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}). Thus, if 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C} the local Gröbner fan defined in 4.1.4 agrees with the analytic standard fan constructed by Assi et al. [ACG01].

Before giving the proof, let us state the last result of this subsection.

Theorem 4.1.9.

Let uu be in 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} and ww be in 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

  • (i)

    For I⊂𝐤⁡[x]I\subset\mathbf{k}[x], gru​(𝐤​[x]0)​inu​(I)=inu​(𝐤​[x]0​I)\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0})\mathrm{in}_{u}(I)=\mathrm{in}_{u}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I).
