    For I⊂𝐤​[x]0I\subset\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}, gru​(O^)​inu​(I)=inu​(O^​I)\mathrm{gr}^{u}({\hat{O}})\mathrm{in}_{u}(I)=\mathrm{in}_{u}({\hat{O}}I).

  • (iii)

    When 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C}, we have similar results concerning (a) I⊂𝐤​[x]0I\subset\mathbf{k}[x]_{0} and inu​(𝒪0​I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(\mathcal{O}_{0}I) and (b) I⊂𝒪0I\subset\mathcal{O}_{0} and inu​(O^​I)\mathrm{in}_{u}({\hat{O}}I).

  • (1)

    For I⊂DI\subset D, grw​(D{0})​inw​(I)=inw​(D{0}​I)\mathrm{gr}^{w}(D_{\{0\}})\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)=\mathrm{in}_{w}(D_{\{0\}}I).

  • (2)

    For I⊂D{0}I\subset D_{\{0\}}, grw​(D^)​inw​(I)=inw​(D^​I)\mathrm{gr}^{w}(\hat{D})\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)=\mathrm{in}_{w}(\hat{D}I).

  • (3)

    When 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C}, we have similar results concerning (a) I⊂D{0}I\subset D_{\{0\}} and inw​(𝒟0​I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(\mathcal{D}_{0}I) and (b) I⊂𝒟0I\subset\mathcal{D}_{0} and inw​(D^​I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(\hat{D}I).

Remark 4.1.10.

By the previous theorem, for I⊂𝐤⁡[x]I\subset\mathbf{k}[x], we have

ℰ⁡(I,𝒰loc)​ is a refinement of ​ℰ​(𝐤​[x]0​I,𝒰loc),\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}})\textrm{ is a refinement of }\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}),

and for II in DD, we have:

ℰ⁡(I,𝒲loc)​ is a refinement of ​ℰ​(D{0}​I,𝒲loc).\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})\textrm{ is a refinement of }\mathcal{E}(D_{\{0\}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).
Proof of Theorem 4.1.9.
  • (1)

    To prove the equality, it is enough to prove the right-left inclusion, the opposite one being trivial. For this, we are reduced to prove: for P∈D{0}​IP\in D_{\{0\}}I, inw​(P)\mathrm{in}_{w}(P) is in the LHS. For such a PP, there exists q⁡(x)∈𝐤⁡[x]q(x)\in\mathbf{k}[x] with q⁡(0)≠0q(0)\neq 0 such that q⁡(x)​P∈Iq(x)P\in I, which implies that inw​(q⁡(x))​inw​(P)∈inw​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(q(x))\mathrm{in}_{w}(P)\in\mathrm{in}_{w}(I). Now inw​(q⁡(x))=inu​(q⁡(x))\mathrm{in}_{w}(q(x))=\mathrm{in}_{u}(q(x)) and since the uiu_{i} are non positive, inu​(q​(x))\mathrm{in}_{u}(q(x)) is invertible in grw​(D{0})\mathrm{gr}^{w}(D_{\{0\}}) (and not only in D{0}D_{\{0\}}).

  • (2)

    The proof for this statement is based on the homogenized version of this theorem to be proved in the next subsection (see Th. 4.2.5). As in (1), only the right-left inclusion is non trivial. Let P∈D^⋅IP\in\hat{D}\cdot I. By lemma 4.2.2 (proved independently in the next subsection), h(𝟎,𝟏)​(P)∈h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)​h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(P)\in h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I). By theorem 4.2.5, inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(P))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(P)) belongs to grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^))​inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I)). We dehomogenize and remark that [inw(h(𝟎,𝟏)(P))]|h=1=inw(P)[\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(P))]_{|h=1}=\mathrm{in}_{w}(P) to conclude.

  • (3)

    (a) is a consequence of (b) and (2) while (b) is a direct consequence of theorem 4.2.5.

∎

Using the previous theorem, let us give the

Proof of Prop. 4.1.8.

Statement (1) follows from the following implication: for any ww, w′w^{\prime}, if inw​(D^​I)⊂inw′​(D^​I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(\hat{D}I)\subset\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(\hat{D}I) then inw​(I)⊂inw′​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)\subset\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I). Let us prove it. By the previous theorem, we are reduced to prove:

(⋆)grw​(D^)​inw​(I)⊂grw​(D^)​inw′​(I)⇒inw​(I)⊂inw′​(I).(\star)\qquad\mathrm{gr}^{w}(\hat{D})\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)\subset\mathrm{gr}^{w}(\hat{D})\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I)\Rightarrow\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)\subset\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I).

This is a direct consequence of the faithful flatness of 𝐤⁡[[x]]\mathbf{k}[[x]] over 𝐤​[x]⟨x1,…,xn⟩\mathbf{k}[x]_{\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle} [Ma89, p. 62].

Let us detail the argument. We take the notations of remark 4.1.1. Let us denote by x~\tilde{x} the set of variables xn2+1,…,xnx_{n_{2}+1},\ldots,x_{n}, and by 𝐤​[x~]⟨x~⟩\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]_{\langle\tilde{x}\rangle} the localization of 𝐤⁡[x~]\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}] w.r.t. the maximal ideal generated by the set x~\tilde{x}. Now, let us first remark that the LHS of (⋆)(\star) implies that for ww and w′w^{\prime}, graded rings are implicitly equal. The LHS of (⋆)(\star) takes place in 𝐤⁡[[x~]]⊗𝐤⁡[x~]grw​(D)\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]]\otimes_{\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]}\mathrm{gr}^{w}(D) and the RHS in 𝐤​[x~]⟨x~⟩⊗𝐤⁡[x~]grw​(D)\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]_{\langle\tilde{x}\rangle}\otimes_{\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]}\mathrm{gr}^{w}(D). Now let us work in the 𝐤​[x~]⟨x~⟩\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]_{\langle\tilde{x}\rangle}-modules category. Then LHS of (⋆)(\star) is equivalent to

𝐤⁡[[x~]]​⨂𝐤​[x~]⟨x~⟩inw​(I)⊂𝐤⁡[[x~]]​⨂𝐤​[x~]⟨x~⟩inw′​(I)\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]]\bigotimes_{\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]_{\langle\tilde{x}\rangle}}\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)\subset\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]]\bigotimes_{\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]_{\langle\tilde{x}\rangle}}\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I)

which is equivalent to the exactness of

0→𝐤⁡[[x~]]​⨂𝐤​[x~]⟨x~⟩inw′​(I)↪(𝐤⁡[[x~]]​⨂𝐤​[x~]⟨x~⟩inw′​(I))+(𝐤⁡[[x~]]​⨂𝐤​[x~]⟨x~⟩inw​(I))→00\rightarrow\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]]\bigotimes_{\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]_{\langle\tilde{x}\rangle}}\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I)\hookrightarrow\Big(\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]]\bigotimes_{\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]_{\langle\tilde{x}\rangle}}\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I)\Big)+\Big(\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]]\bigotimes_{\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]_{\langle\tilde{x}\rangle}}\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)\Big)\rightarrow 0

(where ↪\hookrightarrow means the inclusion) but (𝐤⁡[[x~]]⊗inw′​(I))+(𝐤⁡[[x~]]⊗inw​(I))=𝐤⁡[[x~]]⊗(inw′​(I)+inw​(I))(\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]]\otimes\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I))+(\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]]\otimes\mathrm{in}_{w}(I))=\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]]\otimes\big(\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I)+\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)\big) thus by faithful flatness of 𝐤⁡[[x~]]\mathbf{k}[[\tilde{x}]] over 𝐤​[x~]⟨x~⟩\mathbf{k}[\tilde{x}]_{\langle\tilde{x}\rangle}, the LHS of (⋆)(\star) is equivalent to the exactness of

0→inw′​(I)↪inw′​(I)+inw​(I)→00\rightarrow\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I)\hookrightarrow\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I)+\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)\rightarrow 0

which means that inw​(I)⊂inw′​(I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(I)\subset\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(I), and we are done.

For statement (2), the proof is similar and based on the faithful flatness of O^{\hat{O}} over 𝒪0\mathcal{O}_{0} [Ma89, p. 62]. ∎

4.1.2. On the passage from local to global

We already know (see Remark 4.1.10) that the global Gröbner fan of II is a refinement of the local one (at 00) so we could ask whether we have a passage from local to global.

Given an ideal II in DD, we considered the local Gröbner fan ℰ⁡(D{0}​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(D_{\{0\}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) at 0∈𝐤n0\in\mathbf{k}^{n}. Now, for any x0∈𝐤nx^{0}\in\mathbf{k}^{n}, we can consider the local Gröbner fan of II at the point x0x^{0} which is defined by considering (u,v)∈𝒲loc(u,v)\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}} as weights on the variables xi−xi0x_{i}-x_{i}^{0} and ∂i\partial_{i} (note that by the affine change of coordinates x↦x′=x−x0x\mapsto x^{\prime}=x-x^{0}, the derivations are not affected i.e. ∂∂xi′=∂∂xi\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{\prime}_{i}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}). Another definition is ℰ⁡(D{0}​Ix↦x−x0,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(D_{\{0\}}I_{x\mapsto x-x^{0}},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

The following question is natural: is the global Gröbner fan ℰ⁡(I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) the common refinement of the local ones ? The next example shows that the answer is no.

Example 4.1.11.

Let f=1+x1+x2∈𝐤⁡[x1,x2]f=1+x_{1}+x_{2}\in\mathbf{k}[x_{1},x_{2}]. To simplify, we will talk about open Gröbner cones. The restriction to 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} of the global Gröbner fan is made of 4 cones: {0}\{0\}, C1={u1<0,u2=0}C_{1}=\{u_{1}<0,u_{2}=0\}, C2={u1<0,u2<0}C_{2}=\{u_{1}<0,u_{2}<0\} and C3={u1=0,u2<0}C_{3}=\{u_{1}=0,u_{2}<0\}. Now for x10,x20∈𝐤x_{1}^{0},x_{2}^{0}\in\mathbf{k}, write f=1+x10+x20+(x1−x10)+(x2−x20)f=1+x_{1}^{0}+x_{2}^{0}+(x_{1}-x_{1}^{0})+(x_{2}-x_{2}^{0}). In the case 1+x10+x20≠01+x_{1}^{0}+x_{2}^{0}\neq 0, ff is invertible in 𝐤​[x1,x2]⟨x1−x10,x2−x20⟩\mathbf{k}[x_{1},x_{2}]_{\langle x_{1}-x_{1}^{0},x_{2}-x_{2}^{0}\rangle}, thus the local Gröbner fan is trivial at such a point; that means that it is made of the 4 cones {0},C1,C2,C3\{0\},C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}. Now if 1+x10+x20=01+x_{1}^{0}+x_{2}^{0}=0 then the local Gröbner fan at (x10,x20)(x_{1}^{0},x_{2}^{0}) is made of 6 cones: {0}\{0\}, C1C_{1}, {u1<0,u2<0,u1<u2}\{u_{1}<0,u_{2}<0,u_{1}<u_{2}\}, {u1<0,u2<0,u1=u2}\{u_{1}<0,u_{2}<0,u_{1}=u_{2}\}, {u1<0,u2​<0,u1>​u2}\{u_{1}<0,u_{2}<0,u_{1}>u_{2}\} and C3C_{3}.

Thus the common refinement of the (two) local Gröbner fans is the latter and it is different from the global one.

4.2. With homogenization

Gröbner fans can be described explicitly by using the notion of reduced Gröbner or standard bases. For an ideal II in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x] or in DD it is not possible, in general, to construct reduced Gröbner bases when the order is not a global order, that is when we work with weight vectors having some negative components. That explains why we need to work with one more variable in homogenized rings. In these kind of rings we can compute reduced Gröbner bases for any orders. Another consequence of homogenization is that Gröbner fans of homogenized ideals have convex cones (see [ACG00] and [SST00]).

In this short subsection, we state homogeneous analogues to the results of the preceding section. Most of the proofs are the same and will not be written. First, here are two lemmas useful for the sequel.

Lemma 4.2.1.

For a given ideal I⊂DI\subset D, we can compute h(𝟏,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(I) as follows: take any admissible (global) order ≺\prec and compute a ≺(𝟏,𝟏)\prec_{{(\mathbf{1,1})}}-standard basis GG of II then h(𝟏,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(I) will be generated by the h(𝟏,𝟏)​(P)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(P) for P∈GP\in G.

Sketch of proof.

Let PP be in II. By definition of GG, we can write P=∑jQj​PjP=\sum_{j}Q_{j}P_{j} with Pj∈GP_{j}\in G and Qj∈DQ_{j}\in D with ord(𝟏,𝟏)​(P)≥ord(𝟏,𝟏)​(Qj​Pj)\mathrm{ord}_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(P)\geq\mathrm{ord}_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(Q_{j}P_{j}). The homogenization then gives: h(𝟏,𝟏)​(P)=∑jhord(𝟏,𝟏)​(P)−ord(𝟏,𝟏)​(Qj​Pj)⋅h(𝟏,𝟏)​(Qj)⋅h(𝟏,𝟏)​(Pj)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(P)=\sum_{j}h^{\mathrm{ord}_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(P)-\mathrm{ord}_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(Q_{j}P_{j})}\cdot h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(Q_{j})\cdot h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(P_{j}). Since the set of the h(𝟏,𝟏)​(P)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(P), PP running over II, generates h(𝟏,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(I), we are done. ∎

Lemma 4.2.2.

Given II in DD. We can compute generators of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I) in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D) by homogenizing a ≺(𝟎,𝟏)\prec_{(\mathbf{0,1})}-standard basis of II and we have

h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I)=h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)​h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I).\displaystyle h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I)=h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I).
Sketch of proof.

Let GG be a ≺(𝟎,𝟏)\prec_{(\mathbf{0,1})}-standard basis of II then with the same proof as above, we prove the first statement. Now by using Buchberger SS-criterion, GG is also a ≺(𝟎,𝟏)\prec_{(\mathbf{0,1})}-standard basis of D^​I\hat{D}I which implies that h(𝟎,𝟏)​(G)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(G) also generates h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I). ∎

As it is easy to see, a homogeneous counterpart of Prop. 4.1.5 holds from which follows a counterpart of Cor. 4.1.6 (the proofs are the same and omitted).

Corollary 4.2.3.

For a (𝟎,𝟏){(\mathbf{0,1})}-homogeneous ideal I⊂h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)I\subset h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D), ℰ⁡(I,𝒲loc′)=ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0})​I,𝒲loc′)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime})=\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}})I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\prime}).

Here is the homogeneous version of Prop. 4.1.8.

Proposition 4.2.4.
  • (1)

    For I⊂D{0}I\subset D_{\{0\}}, ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I),𝒲loc)=ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})=\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

  • (2)

    If 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C} and I⊂𝒟0I\subset\mathcal{D}_{0} then ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I),𝒲loc)=ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})=\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

Statement (2) is a direct consequence of 3.3.2 but it can be proved as Prop. 4.1.8. The proof of (1) is almost the same as that of Prop. 4.1.8, providing the fact that h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I)=h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)​h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I)=h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I) (this is Lemma 4.2.2).

Finally, here is the homogeneous counterpart of Th. 4.1.9.

Theorem 4.2.5.

Let ww be in 𝒲loc\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

  • (1)

    For I⊂DI\subset D, grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}))​inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I))=inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}​I))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I))=\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}I)).

  • (2)

    For I⊂D{0}I\subset D_{\{0\}}, grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^))​inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I))=inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I))=\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I)).

  • (3)

    When 𝐤=ℂ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{C}, we have similar results concerning (a) I⊂D{0}I\subset D_{\{0\}} and inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(𝒟0​I))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\mathcal{D}_{0}I)) and (b) I⊂𝒟0I\subset\mathcal{D}_{0} and inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I)).

Remark 4.2.6.

As a consequence of (1) of this theorem, we obtain: for I⊂DI\subset D,

ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I),𝒲loc)​ refines ​ℰ​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}​I),𝒲loc).\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})\text{ refines }\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).
Proof of the Theorem.

Concerning (1), the proof is the same as for Th. 4.1.9. Let us prove (2). By [GOT04, Cor. 3.3] and by the previous lemma, Exp≺wh(h(𝟎,𝟏)(I))=Exp≺wh(h(𝟎,𝟏)(D^I))\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec_{w}^{h}}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I))=\mathrm{Exp}_{\prec_{w}^{h}}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I)). Let GG be a homogeneous ≺wh\prec_{w}^{h}-standard basis of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I). The equality above implies that GG is also a ≺wh\prec_{w}^{h}-standard basis of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I). As a consequence, inw​(G)\mathrm{in}_{w}(G) generates inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I)) over grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}})) and also generates inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I)) over grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})). This implies the desired equality.

Statement (3)(a) is a consequence of (2) and (3)(b). For the latter, consider a standard basis of II w.r.t. the order ⊲wh\lhd_{w}^{h} (see section 3) then the initial forms inw​(⋅)\mathrm{in}_{w}(\cdot) form a system of generators of inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I)) and of inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)​h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I)). Finally, we remark that h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^)​h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)=h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D})h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I)=h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I) which can be easily shown by homogenizing a (𝟎,𝟏){(\mathbf{0,1})}-standard basis of II. ∎

5. Algorithms for local Gröbner fans

In this section, we will focus on the following problems:
Given an ideal II in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x] (resp. in DD), find an algorithm for computing the following local Gröbner fans ℰ¯​(O^​I,𝒰loc∩L)\bar{\mathcal{E}}({\hat{O}}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L) and ℰ¯​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I),𝒲loc∩L)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L)). Here, LL is a linear subspace in a space of weights. Our approach is based on the fact that the local Gröbner fan can be refined by the global Gröbner fan of some homogeneous ideal, the latter being computable.

Since the fans ℰ¯​(O^​I,𝒰loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}({\hat{O}}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) and ℰ¯​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I),𝒲loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) are polyhedral fans, it is enough for obtaining the Gröbner fan restricted to the space LL to enumerate the maximal dimensional cones in the whole weight space. All lower dimensional Gröbner cones are obtained by taking faces of the maximal dimensional cones. We proved that local and global Gröbner cones agree in maximal dimensional strata of the whole weight space. Hence, if we ignore complexity of computation, we do not need to consider the problem of enumerating the local Gröbner cones in a weight space restricted to the linear subspace LL. However, the cost of enumerating all the Gröbner cones in the maximal dimensional strata in the whole weight space is very high in general. For example, for an 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}-hypergeometric system associated to the matrix A=(1,2,3)A=(1,2,3), there are more than 1500 maximal dimensional cones. Our implementation could not finish the enumeration in 3 days. However, the small Gröbner fan, which is a fan restricted to the linear subspace ui+vi=0u_{i}+v_{i}=0, consists of only 77 maximal dimensional cones. This is the main reason why we restrict our weight space to a linear subspace. We note that local and global Gröbner cones do not agree in general in the restricted weight space 𝒲loc∩L\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L. See Example 5.5.1 (see also Ex. 4.1.7).

Finally, let us mention that Jensen has developed a software package called Gfan [Je05] (see also Fukuda et al. [FJT05]), which can compute the (global) Gröbner fan of a polynomial ideal. In [FJT05], the authors propose a theory of Gröbner fans for non-homogeneous ideals, but these fans are not “local”. Indeed it is easy to construct an example of two polynomial ideals having the same Gröbner fan in the sense of [FJT05] and for which the local Gröbner fans are different: in 𝐤⁡[x1,x2]\mathbf{k}[x_{1},x_{2}], consider I1=(g)I_{1}=(g) and I2=(1+g)I_{2}=(1+g) where g=x1+x2+x1​x22+x12​x2g=x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{1}x_{2}^{2}+x_{1}^{2}x_{2}.

5.1. The commutative case

Let II be in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x]. We want an algorithm for ℰ⁡(O^​I,𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}({\hat{O}}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

Theorem 5.1.1.

Suppose there exists a weight vector α∈(ℕ>0)n\alpha\in(\mathbb{N}_{>0})^{n} such that II is α\alpha-homogeneous then

ℰ⁡(O^​I,𝒰loc)=ℰ⁡(I,𝒰loc)∩SO^.\mathcal{E}({\hat{O}}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}})=\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}})\cap S_{\hat{O}}.

In other terms, local and global Gröbner fans coincide up to the stratification by the ring O^{\hat{O}}.

Proof.

It is easy to see that ℰ¯​(I,𝒰glob)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}}) is a polyhedral fan. Indeed the proof is the same as in the known case where α=(1,…,1)\alpha=(1,\ldots,1) (see [St95]). It then implies that ℰ¯​(I,𝒰loc)∩ℰ¯​(O^,𝒰loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}})\cap\bar{\mathcal{E}}({\hat{O}},\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is a fan. Moreover, a polyhedral fan depends only on its maximal cones and by Cor. 4.1.6, local and global Gröbner fans coincide on the interior of 𝒰loc\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}} so ℰ¯​(O^​I,𝒰loc)=ℰ¯​(I,𝒰loc)∩ℰ¯​(O^,𝒰loc)\bar{\mathcal{E}}({\hat{O}}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}})=\bar{\mathcal{E}}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}})\cap\bar{\mathcal{E}}({\hat{O}},\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}). This last equality is equivalent to the one we had to prove. ∎

Now suppose that II is not homogeneous for any positive weight vector. Choose a weight vector α∈(ℕ>0)n\alpha\in(\mathbb{N}_{>0})^{n}. Let {fi,i}\{f_{i},i\} be a given set of generators of II. Let hh be a new variable and let I(h)I^{(h)} be the ideal of 𝐤⁡[x,h]\mathbf{k}[x,h] generated by the set of hα​(fi)h_{\alpha}(f_{i}), where hα​(fi)h_{\alpha}(f_{i}) is the α\alpha-homogenization of fif_{i}.

Proposition 5.1.2.

ℰ⁡(I(h),𝒰glob)\mathcal{E}(I^{(h)},\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}}) refines ℰ⁡(I,𝒰glob)\mathcal{E}(I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{glob}}).

Proof.

Given uu and u′u^{\prime}, we have to prove this implication:

inu​(I(h))=inu′​(I(h))⇒inu​(I)=inu′​(I).\mathrm{in}_{u}(I^{(h)})=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(I^{(h)})\Rightarrow\mathrm{in}_{u}(I)=\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(I).

Suppose the LHS true. Let ff be in II and let us prove that inu​(f)∈inu′​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(f)\in\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(I). Let us write f=∑iqi​fif=\sum_{i}q_{i}f_{i}. By homogenizing, we obtain: there exists ll and lil_{i} for any ii such that

hl​hα​(f)=∑ihli​hα​(qi)​hα​(fi)h^{l}h_{\alpha}(f)=\sum_{i}h^{l_{i}}h_{\alpha}(q_{i})h_{\alpha}(f_{i})

so hl​hα​(f)h^{l}h_{\alpha}(f) belongs to I(h)I^{(h)}. By taking the initial form w.r.t. uu, we obtain by hypothesis: inu​(hl​hα​(f))=∑jrj​inu′​(gj)\mathrm{in}_{u}(h^{l}h_{\alpha}(f))=\sum_{j}r_{j}\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(g_{j}) with gj∈I(h)g_{j}\in I^{(h)}. It suffices to set h=1h=1 to obtain the desired relation. Thus this inclusion holds: inu​(I)⊂inu′​(I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(I)\subset\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(I). The reverse inclusion holds by symmetry which ends the proof. ∎

Combining this proposition with Rem. 4.1.10, we obtain:

Corollary 5.1.3.

The fan ℰ⁡(I(h),𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}(I^{(h)},\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}) refines ℰ⁡(𝐤​[x]0​I,𝒰loc)\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

Algorithm 5.1.4 (Computation of ℰ¯​(𝐤​[x]0​I,𝒰loc∩L){\bar{\mathcal{E}}}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L)).


Input: an ideal II in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x]. A linear subspace LL in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.
Output: the local Gröbner fan ℰ¯​(𝐤​[x]0​I,𝒰loc∩L){\bar{\mathcal{E}}}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L).
Step 1:

Compute the set Σ0\Sigma_{0} of maximal cones of the global Gröbner fan of I(h)I^{(h)} restricted to 𝒰loc∩L\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L: ℰ⁡(I(h),𝒰loc∩L)\mathcal{E}(I^{(h)},\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L).

Step 2:

For any C,C′∈Σ0C,C^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{0}, using an écart division, compare inu​(𝐤​[x]0​I)\mathrm{in}_{u}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I) and inu′​(𝐤​[x]0​I)\mathrm{in}_{u^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I) in gru​(𝐤​[x]0)\mathrm{gr}_{u}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}) for some u∈Cu\in C, u′∈C′u^{\prime}\in C^{\prime}. If it is equal, glue CC and C′C^{\prime}. By continuing this process, we construct the set Σ\Sigma of maximal cones of ℰ¯​(𝐤​[x]0​I,𝒰loc∩L){\bar{\mathcal{E}}}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0}I,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L). From Σ\Sigma, construct the set ℰ\mathcal{E} of all the cones.

Output ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Let us add two remarks to the algorithm.

The step 1 can be performed by flipping of the maximal dimensional cones in the linear space LL with respect to the facets. As to details, see Algorithm 3.6 of the book by Sturmfels [St95]. Note that the correctness of the flipping procedure for the enumeration comes from the fact that the Gröbner fan is a polyhedral fan. The flipping procedure can be accelarated by Collart-Kalkbrener-Mall’s Gröbner walk method [CKM97]. We note that the method also works in rings of differential operators.

The second remark is on the écart division in Step 2. Suppose that supp​u=supp​u′={1,2,…,m}\mathrm{supp}\,u=\mathrm{supp}\,u^{\prime}=\{1,2,\ldots,m\}. Then, we have

gru(𝐤[x]0)≃{f/g|f∈𝐤[x],g∈𝐤[xm+1,…,xn],g(0)≠0}.\mathrm{gr}^{u}(\mathbf{k}[x]_{0})\simeq\left\{f/g|f\in\mathbf{k}[x],g\in\mathbf{k}[x_{m+1},\ldots,x_{n}],g(0)\not=0\right\}.

The écart division in literatures usually suppose that denominators are in 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x], but our denominator gg lies in 𝐤⁡[xm+1,…,xn]\mathbf{k}[x_{m+1},\ldots,x_{n}]. Hence, in our case, a reducer must be chosen so that the multiplier monomial for the pseudo-division is in the ring 𝐤⁡[xm+1,…,xn]\mathbf{k}[x_{m+1},\ldots,x_{n}] instead of 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x] as in the case of the usual écart division [Mo82], [Gr94], [GP96].

5.2. The non homogeneous case

Proposition 5.2.1.

Let II be in DD then ℰ​(h(𝟏,𝟏)​(I),W)\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(I),W) refines ℰ⁡(I,W)\mathcal{E}(I,W) for any W⊂𝒲globW\subset\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{glob}}.

In fact, we have a more general result. Let GG be any system of generators of II over DD and let I(h)⊂h(𝟏,𝟏)​(D)I^{(h)}\subset h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(D) be generated by {h(𝟏,𝟏)​(P)|P∈G}\{h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(P)|P\in G\} (of course, this ideal is not uniquely determined).

Remark 5.2.2 (On the computation of ℰ⁡(I(h),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(I^{(h)},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})).

Since I(h)I^{(h)} is homogeneous, it is well known that its Gröbner fan can be computed by using reduced Gröbner bases w.r.t. to well-orders (see e.g. [SST00]).

Proposition 5.2.3.

The fan ℰ⁡(I(h),W)\mathcal{E}(I^{(h)},W) refines ℰ⁡(I,W)\mathcal{E}(I,W) (for W⊂𝒲globW\subset\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{glob}}).

Proof.

The same as that of Prop. 5.1.2. ∎

Now combining the previous proposition with Remark 4.1.10, we obtain:

Corollary 5.2.4.

The fan ℰ⁡(I(h),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(I^{(h)},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is a refinement of ℰ⁡(D{0}​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(D_{\{0\}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

By this Corollary, we obtain the following algorithm.

Algorithm 5.2.5 (Computation of ℰ⁡(D{0}​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(D_{\{0\}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})).


Input: an ideal II in DD.
Output: the local Gröbner fan ℰ⁡(D{0}​I,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(D_{\{0\}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).
Step 1:

Compute one of the two (global) Gröbner fans and call it ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0}:
∙\bullet ℰ⁡(h(𝟏,𝟏)​(I),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) (see Lemma 4.2.1 for how to compute h(𝟏,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(I))
∙\bullet ℰ⁡(I(h),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(I^{(h)},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})
This computation can be done as in [SST00, Chapter 2].

Step 2:

Two cones CC and C′C^{\prime} of ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} are said to be in a same class if for one w∈Cw\in C and one w′∈C′w^{\prime}\in C^{\prime}, we have inw​(D{0}​I)=inw′​(D{0}​I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(D_{\{0\}}I)=\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(D_{\{0\}}I).
By using Algorithm 5.2.6, compute the classes of ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0}.
Set ℰ:=\mathcal{E}:=the set of the classes of ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0}.

Output ℰ\mathcal{E}.

We note that ℰ¯​(D{0}​I,𝒲loc){\bar{\mathcal{E}}}(D_{\{0\}}I,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is not a polyhedral fan in general. Hence, we need to perform the merging procedure in Step 2 for all dimensional Gröbner cones.

Algorithm 5.2.6.


Input: I⊂DI\subset D, w,w′∈𝒲locw,w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}
Output : 11 if inw​(D{0}​I)=inw′​(D{0}​I)\mathrm{in}_{w}(D_{\{0\}}I)=\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(D_{\{0\}}I) and 00 if not.
(1) Compute G1G_{1} a ww-standard basis of II and G2G_{2} a w′w^{\prime}-standard basis of II.
(2) By a reduction via an écart (division as in [GOT04]), compare G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}

Let us make some remarks on Algorithm 5.2.6: Concerning step (1), the following fact is basic: Let H1H_{1} (resp. H2H_{2}) be the reduced Gröbner basis of I(h)I^{(h)} w.r.t. a well order that privileges ww (resp. w′w^{\prime}). Then by the specialization h=1h=1 we can set Gi=Hi|h=1G_{i}={H_{i}}_{|h=1}. Thus Step (1) does not require extra computations since the reduced Gröbner basis of I(h)I^{(h)} were needed in Algorithm 5.2.5.

For Step (2), we can use two methods. The first one is an écart division in DD as in [GOT04] (which works although the écart division of loc. cit. is stated in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D)). The second method is based on the following equivalence

inw​(D{0}​I)=inw′​(D{0}​I)⇔(inw​(D{0}​I))(h)=(inw′​(D{0}​I))(h).\mathrm{in}_{w}(D_{\{0\}}I)=\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(D_{\{0\}}I)\iff(\mathrm{in}_{w}(D_{\{0\}}I))^{(h)}=(\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(D_{\{0\}}I))^{(h)}.

The right-left implication can be proved in a similar way as that of Prop. 5.1.2, while the left-right one is trivial. Using this equivalence, we can use écart division in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D).

5.3. The doubly homogenized Weyl algebra

In the next subsection, we present two variants for an algorithm of computing the Gröbner fan of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I). One variant is based on the doubly homogenized Weyl algebra that we introduce here.

The doubly homogenized Weyl algebra h′​(D)h^{\prime}(D) is generated by

x1,…,xn,∂1,…,∂n,h,h′x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n},h,h^{\prime}

with the relations

∂ixi=xi∂i+hh′.\partial_{i}x_{i}=x_{i}\partial_{i}+hh^{\prime}.

Let ≺\prec be a total order on the set of normally ordered monomials xα​∂βhp​h′qx^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{p}{h^{\prime}}^{q} in h′​(D)h^{\prime}(D). Such an order is called a multiplicative monomial order if the following two conditions hold:
1. xi∂i≻hh′x_{i}\partial_{i}\succ hh^{\prime} for i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\ldots,n;
2. xα​∂βhk​h′l≺xα′​∂β′hk′​h′l′x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{k}{h^{\prime}}^{l}\prec x^{\alpha^{\prime}}\partial^{\beta^{\prime}}h^{k^{\prime}}{h^{\prime}}^{l^{\prime}} ⟹\Longrightarrow xα+a​∂β+bhk+q​h′l+r≺xα′+a​∂β′+bhk′+q​h′l′+rx^{\alpha+a}\partial^{\beta+b}h^{k+q}{h^{\prime}}^{l+r}\prec x^{\alpha^{\prime}+a}\partial^{\beta^{\prime}+b}h^{k^{\prime}+q}{h^{\prime}}^{l^{\prime}+r}. Under this definition, the theory of Gröbner basis works analogously with DD for this ring. The Gröbner fan is also defined analogously. We denote by tt a weight for hh and by t′t^{\prime} a weight for h′h^{\prime}.

Theorem 5.3.1.

Consider the weight space

ui+vi≥t+t′u_{i}+v_{i}\geq t+t^{\prime}

and fix a homogeneous left ideal JJ in h′​(D)h^{\prime}(D). The collection of closures of the Gröbner cones of JJ in the weight space is a polyhedral fan.

The proof is analogous to the case of h(𝟏,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(D) (see [SST00]). Indeed with the definitions below we dispose of a well order and reduced Gröbner bases exist. As for Prop. 5.1.2, we have:

Proposition 5.3.2.

If we restrict the fan to the linear subspace t=t′=0t=t^{\prime}=0, then it is a refinement of the Gröbner fan of J|h′=1J_{|h^{\prime}=1} in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D)

Let ≺1\prec_{1} be a multiplicative monomial order in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D) satisfying (2.1), (2.2), (2.3) of [GOT04]:

  1. (1)

    xi∂i≻1hx_{i}\partial_{i}\succ_{1}h.

  2. (2)

    if |β|+k<|β′|+k′|\beta|+k<|\beta^{\prime}|+k^{\prime} then xα∂βhk≺1xα′∂β′hk′x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{k}\prec_{1}x^{\alpha^{\prime}}\partial^{\beta^{\prime}}h^{k^{\prime}}.

  3. (3)

    xα⪯1x^{\alpha}\preceq 1.

We define an order on h′​(D)h^{\prime}(D) as a block order on ≺1\prec_{1} as follows:

(6) xα​∂βhk​h′l≺xα′​∂β′hk′​h′l′⇔{|α|+|β|+k+l<|α′|+|β′|+k′+l′or = and xα∂βhk≺1xα′∂β′hk′.x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{k}{h^{\prime}}^{l}\prec x^{\alpha^{\prime}}\partial^{\beta^{\prime}}h^{k^{\prime}}{h^{\prime}}^{l^{\prime}}\Leftrightarrow\begin{cases}|\alpha|+|\beta|+k+l<|\alpha^{\prime}|+|\beta^{\prime}|+k^{\prime}+l^{\prime}\\ \textrm{or }=\textrm{ and }x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{k}\prec_{1}x^{\alpha^{\prime}}\partial^{\beta^{\prime}}h^{k^{\prime}}.\end{cases}
Lemma 5.3.3.

Let f,g∈h′​(D)f,g\in{h^{\prime}}(D) be homogeneous and ≺\prec be an order satisfying (6). If exp≺⁡(f)⪯exp≺⁡(g)\exp_{\prec}(f)\preceq\exp_{\prec}(g), then exp≺1(f|h′=1)⪯1exp≺1(g|h′=1)\exp_{\prec_{1}}(f_{|h^{\prime}=1})\preceq_{1}\exp_{\prec_{1}}(g_{|h^{\prime}=1}).

This lemma does not hold for h′↦hh^{\prime}\mapsto h.

Proof.

Suppose that lm≺​(f)\mathrm{lm}_{\prec}(f) is equal to c​xα​∂βhk​h′lcx^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{k}{h^{\prime}}^{l}. Since ff is homogeneous and ≺\prec is a block order, the leading monomial of f|h′=1f_{|h^{\prime}=1} is lm≺1(f|h′=1)=cxα∂βhk\mathrm{lm}_{\prec_{1}}(f_{|h^{\prime}=1})=cx^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}h^{k}. In other words, cancelation does not happen when h′↦1h^{\prime}\mapsto 1. It completes the proof. ∎

Theorem 5.3.4.

Fix a homogeneous left ideal JJ in h′​(D)h^{\prime}(D) generated by FF. Let ≺1\prec_{1} be an ordering in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D) satisfying (2.1), (2.2), (2.3) of [GOT04]: Let GG be a Gröbner basis of II for the order ≺\prec defined as in (6). Then, the dehomogenization G|h′=1G_{|h^{\prime}=1} is a standard basis in the sense of [GOT04, Def. 3.1] of the ideal generated by F|h′=1F_{|h^{\prime}=1} with respect to the order ≺1\prec_{1}.

Proof.

G|h′=1G_{|h^{\prime}=1} generates the ideal generated by F|h′=1F_{|h^{\prime}=1} since GG generates the ideal generated by FF. Denote the elements of GG by {gi}\{g_{i}\}. Since GG is a Gröbner basis, we have Buchberger’s S-pair criterion;

sp⁡(gi,gj)=∑kqi​j​k​gk,exp≺⁡(sp⁡(gi,gj))⪰exp≺⁡(qi​j​k​gk).{\rm sp}(g_{i},g_{j})=\sum_{k}q_{ijk}g_{k},\quad\exp_{\prec}({\rm sp}(g_{i},g_{j}))\succeq\exp_{\prec}(q_{ijk}g_{k}).

It follows from Lemma 5.3.3 that sp(gi,gj)|h′=1=∑kqi​j​k|h′=1gk|h′=1{\rm sp}(g_{i},g_{j})_{|h^{\prime}=1}=\sum_{k}{q_{ijk}}_{|h^{\prime}=1}{g_{k}}_{|h^{\prime}=1} with

exp≺1(sp(gi,gj)|h′=1)⪰1exp≺1((qi​j​kgk)|h′=1).\exp_{\prec_{1}}({\rm sp}(g_{i},g_{j})_{|h^{\prime}=1})\succeq_{1}\exp_{\prec_{1}}((q_{ijk}g_{k})_{|h^{\prime}=1}).

Then, by Theorem 3.2 of [GOT04], we conclude the theorem. ∎

5.4. The homogeneous case

Denote by J1J_{1} the ideal of h′​(D)h^{\prime}(D) generated by homogenization of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I) with the variable h′h^{\prime} (in fact we homogenize any set of generators of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I)). The ideal J1J_{1} is homogeneous in the doubly homogenized Weyl algebra h′​(D)h^{\prime}(D). Combining Proposition 5.3.2 and Remark 4.2.6, we have:

Corollary 5.4.1.

The fan ℰ⁡(J1,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(J_{1},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is a refinement of ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}​I),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

This Corollary gives a first variant for computing local Gröbner fan. Let us explain the second variant. Now, we use the notions of [GOT04]: for P∈h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)P\in h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D), we denote by P(s)P^{(s)} the (−𝟏,𝟏)(\mathbf{-1,1})-homogenization in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)​[s]h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D)[s] (here ss is a new variable commuting with the other ones). Let GG be a set of generators of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I) over h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D), then define h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)(s)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I)^{(s)} as the ideal of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)​[s]h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D)[s] generated by P(s)P^{(s)} for P∈GP\in G. To simplify denote by J2J_{2} this ideal.

Then we can consider the Gröbner fan ℰ⁡(J2,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(J_{2},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) as we did before, by putting a weight 00 on ss.

Remark 5.4.2 (On the computation of ℰ⁡(J,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(J,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}})).

In h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)​[s]h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D)[s] we dispose of a well-order ≺s\prec_{s} (notation of [GOT04]), thus the Gröbner fan of JJ can be computed via reduced Gröbner bases computations.

Proposition 5.4.3.

The fan ℰ⁡(J2,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(J_{2},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is a refinement of ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

We omit the proof since it is similar to that of Prop. 5.1.2. By Prop. 5.4.3 and Remark 4.2.6:

Corollary 5.4.4.

The fan ℰ⁡(J2,𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(J_{2},\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}) is a refinement of ℰ⁡(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}​I),𝒲loc)\mathcal{E}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}).

As a consequence, we obtain the next algorithm.

Algorithm 5.4.5 (Computation of ℰ¯​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}​I),𝒲loc∩L){\bar{\mathcal{E}}}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L)).


Input: an ideal II in DD. A linear subspace LL in ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n}.
Output: the local Gröbner fan ℰ¯​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}​I),𝒲loc∩L){\bar{\mathcal{E}}}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}I),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L).
Step 1:

Compute the set Σ0\Sigma_{0} of the maximal cones of the global Gröbner fan ℰ¯​(J,𝒲loc∩L){\bar{\mathcal{E}}}(J,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L) where JJ is one of J1,J2J_{1},J_{2}.

Step 2:

As before, compute the classes of Σ0\Sigma_{0}, by using Algorithm 5.4.6.
From the set of the classes of Σ0\Sigma_{0}, construct the set ℰ\mathcal{E} of all the cones of ℰ⁡(J,𝒲loc∩L)\mathcal{E}(J,\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L).

Output ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Algorithm 5.4.6.


Input: I⊂DI\subset D, w,w′∈𝒲locw,w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}
Output : 11 if inw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}​I))=inw′​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}​I))\mathrm{in}_{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}I))=\mathrm{in}_{w^{\prime}}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}I)) and 00 if not.
(1) Compute G1G_{1} a ww-standard basis of II and G2G_{2} a w′w^{\prime}-standard basis of h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I).
(2) By a reduction via an écart division in grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D)) as in [GOT04], compare G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}.

Let us give some remarks on this algorithm.
- As before, we can obtain G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} by dehomogenizing operators computed in Algorithm 5.4.5. The justification of Step (1) lies in the fact that h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I) generates h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0}​I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}I) over h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D{0})h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D_{\{0\}}). Moreover we have seen in Lemma 4.2.2 how to compute h(𝟎,𝟏)​(I)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(I).
- The écart division of [GOT04] (stated in h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D)) works well in grw​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D))\mathrm{gr}^{w}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(D)) with a modification; a reducer must be chosen so that the multiplier monomial for the pseudo division is in the ring 𝐤⁡[xm+1,…,xn]\mathbf{k}[x_{m+1},\ldots,x_{n}] instead of 𝐤⁡[x]\mathbf{k}[x] as in the case of the usual écart division. Here, we assume that Supp⁡(u)={1,…,m}{\rm Supp}(u)=\{1,\ldots,m\}.
- Finally, since ℰ¯​(h(𝟎,𝟏)​(D^​I)),𝒲loc\bar{\mathcal{E}}(h_{(\mathbf{0,1})}(\hat{D}I)),\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}} is a polyhedral fan, it is enough, in step 1, to compute only the maximal cones.

5.5. Tips for implementation and examples

We implemented the algorithms except Algorithm 5.2.5 in this paper in a combination of Kan [Ta91] and Polymake [GJ]. The following is a list of known implementations for Gröbner fans and some efficiency studies including Gröbner walk.

  1. (1)

    Macaulay [BS] command hull implemented by A. Reebs constructs state polytopes.

  2. (2)

    The Singular developing team [GPS04] implements the Gröbner walk techniques [CKM97], [FGLM93].

  3. (3)

    B. Huber and R. Thomas gave an efficient algorithm and implementation specialized to getting Gröbner fan for toric ideals [HT00].

Our implementation is new in view of the following aspects.

  1. (1)

    It is the first implementation for local Gröbner fans.

  2. (2)

    Computation is split into a system for algebra (Kan) and a system for geometry (Polymake). They are connected by the OpenXM-RFC 104 protocol (OoHG, OpenXM on HTTP/GET) [OpenXM]. This design gives us a robust system, since the polymake is a strong, flexible, and robust system for polytopes developed by E. Gawrilow and M. Joswig linked with GMP and cdd by K. Fukuda. We use polymake properties DIM, FACETS, INEQUALITIES.

We have explained our algorithms for local Gröbner fans in the previous sections. The dominant part in the computation time is Step 1’s. Let us explain some details of Step 1, which obtains the maximal dimensional Gröbner cones in a homogenized ring.

  1. (1)

    Parametrize the weight space 𝒲loc∩L\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L by a polyhedron W⊆ℝdim⁡(𝒲loc∩L)W\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}^{{\rm dim}\,(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L)}. The parameterization is given by a matrix WconeW_{\rm cone}.

  2. (2)

    Find a starting weight vector uu such that the dimension of the (projected) Gröbner cone C⁡[u]⊆WC[u]\subseteq W is dim⁡(𝒲loc∩L){\rm dim}\,(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L).

  3. (3)

    If C⁡[u]C[u] is not pointed, then there exists a non-zero linear space in C⁡[u]C[u]. Let LconeL_{\rm cone} be the maximal linear space in C⁡[u]C[u]. We construct Gröbner cones in W/LconeW/L_{\rm cone}. In other words we work in the othogonal space to LconeL_{\rm cone}. It is necessary because the Polymake and polyhedral algorithms works efficiently only for pointed cones. Note that all maximal dimensional cones in the WW space contain the linear space LconeL_{\rm cone} since the Gröbner fan is a polyhedral fan.

  4. (4)

    Enumerate the facets of C⁡[u]/LconeC[u]/L_{\rm cone}. They are either on the border of W/LconeW/L_{\rm cone} or not.

  5. (5)

    Perturb the weight vector uu with respect to a facet FF, which is not on the border of the weight space WW, as explained in [St95, Chapter 3].

  6. (6)

    Lift the new weight vector in W/LconeW/L_{\rm cone} to 𝒲loc∩L\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{loc}}\cap L. Let u′u^{\prime} be the lifted weight vector. Construct the new reduced Gröbner basis and construct C⁡[u′]/LconeC[u^{\prime}]/L_{\rm cone}. If C⁡[u]/Lcone∩C⁡[u′]/LconeC[u]/L_{\rm cone}\cap C[u^{\prime}]/L_{\rm cone} is the facet FF, then we mark the facet FF as flipped, else retry to get a new u′u^{\prime} with a smaller ε\varepsilon perturbation.

  7. (7)

    Continue the procedure of getting new Gröbner cones and new facets until all facets have been marked with flipped.

As to more details, see the source code gfan.sm1 of our test implementation.

Remark.

In the computations above, the local Gröbner fans are trivial: i.e. there is no slope between v1=(−1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0)v_{1}=(-1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0) and v2=(0,−1,0,0,0,1,0,0)v_{2}=(0,-1,0,0,0,1,0,0). The global Gröbner fans are not trivial: there is the slope L12=⟨(1,1)⟩=⟨1⋅v1+1⋅v2⟩L_{12}=\langle(1,1)\rangle=\langle 1\cdot v_{1}+1\cdot v_{2}\rangle. This may be explained by the following: The only point where the local Bernstein-Sato is not “trivial” (in some sense) is (1,0)(1,0) because for any (x0,y0)≠(1,0)(x_{0},y_{0})\neq(1,0), f1f_{1} or f2f_{2} becomes a unit in 𝒪(x0,y0)\mathcal{O}_{(x_{0},y_{0})}. Now in local coordinates (x′,y′)(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}) around (1,0)(1,0), (f1,f2)(f_{1},f_{2}) is written as (y′,y′−x′2)(y^{\prime},y^{\prime}-x^{\prime 2}) and the Bernstein-Sato ideal is known to be generated by (s1+1)​(s2+1)​(2​s1+2​s2+3)​(2​s1+2​s2+5)(s_{1}+1)(s_{2}+1)(2s_{1}+2s_{2}+3)(2s_{1}+2s_{2}+5). We then clearly see the linear form (or the slope) (1,1)(1,1).

This example tries to show how far we can enumerate Gröbner cones with our implementation. Let ℓk\ell_{k} be a differential operator

ℓk=∂xk−(∑i=1nxi∂xi+1/2)(xk∂xk+1/(2k+1)).\ell_{k}=\partial_{x_{k}}-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\partial_{x_{i}}+1/2\right)\left(x_{k}\partial_{x_{k}}+1/(2k+1)\right).

We consider the ideal IhI^{h} in the homogenized Weyl algebra h(𝟏,𝟏)​(D)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(D) in nn variables generated by h(𝟏,𝟏)​(ℓ1),…,h(𝟏,𝟏)​(ℓn)h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(\ell_{1}),\ldots,h_{(\mathbf{1,1})}(\ell_{n}), which is a system of differential equations for a Lauricella hypergeometric series with irregular singularities when h=1h=1.

Example 5.5.3.

In our experience, computation in the doubly homogenized Weyl algebra h′​(D)h^{\prime}(D) sometimes exhausts huge memory space. For example, consider the left ideal generated by

x3+y2​h′−t1​h′2,y3+x2​h′−t2​h′2,3​x2​∂t1+2​x​h′​∂t2+h′2​∂x,3​y2​∂t2+2​y​h′​∂t1+h′2​∂yx^{3}+y^{2}h^{\prime}-t_{1}{h^{\prime}}^{2},y^{3}+x^{2}h^{\prime}-t_{2}{h^{\prime}}^{2},3x^{2}\partial{t_{1}}+2xh^{\prime}\partial{t_{2}}+{h^{\prime}}^{2}\partial{x},3y^{2}\partial{t_{2}}+2yh^{\prime}\partial{t_{1}}+{h^{\prime}}^{2}\partial{y}

in the doubly homogenized Weyl algebra 𝐐⁡⟨h,h′,x,y,t1,t2,∂x,∂y,∂t1,∂t2⟩{\bf Q}\langle h,h^{\prime},x,y,t_{1},t_{2},\partial{x},\partial{y},\partial{t_{1}},\partial{t_{2}}\rangle. We want to get the Gröbner fan in the restricted weight space

{(0,0,−w1,−w2,0,0,w1,w2)|wi≥0},where −wi stands for ti\{(0,0,-w_{1},-w_{2},0,0,w_{1},w_{2})\,|\,w_{i}\geq 0\},\quad\mbox{where $-w_{i}$ stands for $t_{i}$}

to compute a Bernstein-Sato polynomial for polynomials x3+y2x^{3}+y^{2} and x2+y3x^{2}+y^{3} with the method given in [Ba05]. However, our implementation exhausts 2G bytes of memory in the stage of constructing the reduced Gröbner basis from a Gröbner basis of Collart-Kalkbrener-Mall’s Gröbner walk.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
